That sounds simple, and it should be simple. But simplicity here is the result of a lot of careful design.

Leasey Texts can tell you what has been inserted. It can optionally speak the name of the Leasey Text, or the full expanded text. It can play a sound when an abbreviation expands. It can add a trailing space so you can continue typing immediately. It can expand abbreviations before punctuation, so if you type an abbreviation followed by a comma or full-stop or period, the full text can be inserted and the punctuation placed correctly afterwards.

For a JAWS user, that spoken or Braille confirmation is important. If you type an abbreviation in the middle of an email, web form, document, chat message or support system, you need to know with confidence that the expected text has been inserted. Leasey Texts is designed to give you that confidence.

A More Flexible Abbreviation System.

Each Leasey Text can have its own abbreviation settings.

You can decide whether the abbreviation is enabled.

You can decide whether it is case sensitive.

You can decide whether Leasey should speak anything after the expansion.

You can decide whether it should speak the name of the Leasey Text or the full expanded text.

You can decide whether a sound should be played.

You can decide whether a trailing space should be added.

This matters because not all stored text is used in the same way.

If the abbreviation inserts a short phrase, you might want Leasey to speak the full text. If it inserts several paragraphs, hearing the whole thing every time would soon become tedious, so you may prefer to hear only the name. If the text is inserted frequently in a busy working environment, a short sound and a spoken confirmation may be enough. If it is used in punctuation-heavy writing, expansion before punctuation can make the process feel much more fluent.

The idea is not just to store text. The idea is to make stored text fit naturally into how you work. We even have plenty of sounds for you to choose from!

Creating and Organising Text.

There are several ways of working with Leasey Texts.

The simple list is still available for quickly inserting a stored item.

If text is already on the Windows Clipboard, you can store it quickly as a Leasey Text.

The main Leasey Texts interface is available when you want more control.

From the main interface, you can create a new Leasey Text, edit an existing one, add or change an abbreviation, assign a category, choose speech and sound behaviour, search the list, and organise items more carefully.

Categories are optional. Some people will want one straight list. Others will want categories such as Work, Personal, Email, Forms, Addresses, Technical Support or Training. Both approaches are valid. Leasey Texts allows the list to grow without becoming unmanageable.

There is also an import process for people who used the previous Leasey Texts system. When the new application starts for the first time, it attempts to import existing texts and abbreviations where they are available. You can also run the import manually from Options.

Clipboard History.

Clipboard History is the second part of the new Leasey Texts application.

When Leasey Texts is running, text copied to the Windows Clipboard can be stored in a history list. You can then review recent clipboard entries and use them again.

We should be very clear about what this feature is intended to be.

There are other clipboard management applications available, some free and some commercial. Some of them do many highly sophisticated things. They may store many different data types, provide complex filtering, synchronise in specialist ways, or offer features for particular professional workflows.

Leasey Clipboard History is not trying to compete with those applications feature for feature.

That is not because the technical work would be impossible. It is because our aim is different.

The aim is to provide a clipboard history feature which is easy to understand, easy to operate with JAWS, and integrated into an application many Leasey users are already permitted to run. A number of organisations have approved Leasey for installation in the workplace. Users have told us that they wanted clipboard history as part of Leasey precisely because installing another clipboard manager may not be possible in their environment.

So the design question becomes: what can we provide that is useful every day without creating another complicated application people have to learn?

Reviewing and Pasting Recent Clipboard Entries.

Clipboard History gives you several practical ways to retrieve recent copied text.

You can open the full Clipboard History tab.

You can open a simple paste list.

You can paste one of the ten most recent clipboard entries directly using shortcut keys.

This is useful in many everyday situations.

Suppose you copy a phone number from one message, a name from another, and a reference number from a web page. Without clipboard history, copying the third item means the first two have gone unless you pasted them somewhere first. With Clipboard History, those copied entries can remain available.

You can bring up the list, choose the item you want, and paste it into the application where you are working.

There are also shortcuts for the ten most recent entries. By default, Alt+Shift+1 pastes the most recent entry, Alt+Shift+2 pastes the second most recent entry, and so on through to Alt+Shift+0 for the tenth. If you know the order in which you copied items, this can be extremely fast.

Monitoring for Clipboard Entries can be stopped at any time, perhaps for security reasons or in the event you wish to use an alternative Clipboard Manager.

Clipboard Entry Properties.

You can open the Properties of an entry by pressing Enter on it. That allows you to review the text a character or a word at a time.

However, it is also possible to edit the text if necessary or rename the entry title.

If the Clipboard Entry contains links or paths to folders, those too can be launched directly from Properties.

Marking Clipboard Entries.

Clipboard History also allows entries to be marked.

You can mark more than one clipboard entry and then copy or paste them together. You can choose how marked items are separated when they are combined. Options include a space, comma, full-stop or period, vertical bar, line break or paragraph break.

This is a small feature with a lot of possible uses.

You might copy several lines from a web page and combine them into a note.

You might gather a name, address and telephone number from different places.

You might collect several short answers from a document.

You might copy a list of items and paste them one at a time into separate fields.

The point is that Clipboard History is not only a safety net for the last thing copied. It can become a simple collecting tool.

Usefully, you can also mark clipboard entries so they can be pasted in a precise order.

Mark the clipboard entries in the order you want to paste them.

Move into the chosen edit area, such as a number of form fields.

Each time you press Control+V, a Clipboard Entry is pasted in the order in which they were copied and JAWS confirms this.

Converting Clipboard Entries.

A Clipboard History item can also be converted into a Leasey Text.

That means if you copy something and realise you will need it again in future, you can turn it into a permanent stored text without starting from scratch.

It can also be converted into a Leasey Clip, making the feature part of the wider Leasey ecosystem rather than an isolated clipboard list.

Both these utilities ensure that the Clipboard History feature is fully integrated into other features the product already has available.

Leasey Media Centre: Podcasts Take a Big Step Forward.

Leasey Media Centre was one of the most ambitious parts of the Summer release. It brought together radio, podcasts, local audio, playlists, recording, sound control and a dedicated media player designed with JAWS users in mind.

For the September update, podcasts have received the most attention.

The change may sound simple at first: Leasey can optionally create a temporary playback copy of a podcast episode before playing it. But that one change unlocks several important benefits.

Until now, the default method of playing a podcast episode was streaming. Streaming is immediate and convenient. You choose an episode, press Enter, and Leasey plays it directly from the internet.

Streaming still exists.

However, Leasey can now also download an episode into a temporary listening area and play that copy automatically. This is not the same as saving the episode permanently. It is a temporary playback copy designed to improve the listening experience.

Why Temporary Playback Copies Matter.

A temporary playback copy can make several features more reliable:

  • Podcast chapters.
  • Bookmarks.
  • Saved playback positions.
  • Automatic resuming.
  • Movement through the episode.
  • Continued playback after the initial download has completed. This is especially valuable for long podcasts. If you listen to a ten-minute item, you may not care much about chapter marks or saved positions. If you listen to a one-hour interview, a two-hour technology podcast, a lecture, a radio documentary or an audio course, those features become far more important.

With the right options enabled, you can start listening to a podcast, stop after 25 minutes, return later, press Enter on the episode, and Leasey can resume from approximately where you stopped.

The saved position belongs to the episode. You do not need to create a bookmark manually just to return to where you left off.

We strongly recommend trying temporary playback copies unless you have a particular reason to stream directly from the internet every time.

Saving Podcast Episodes Permanently.

Temporary playback copies are for listening. They are not the same as episodes you deliberately save and keep.

The September update also improves the process of saving podcast episodes permanently.

You can save one episode, but you can also save multiple episodes. This is useful if you are going on a journey, preparing for a period without reliable internet, archiving a series, or collecting material for later listening.

Leasey provides progress information while saving. It also gives you a way to cancel before saving if you realise you have chosen the wrong item or too many episodes.

Again, the goal is not merely to provide the function. The goal is to make the process understandable while it is happening.

Filtering the Episode List.

The podcast episode list can now be filtered in several different ways: all episodes, played episodes, unplayed episodes and those which are in progress; in other words, those you have partly heard.

Podcast Chapter Marks Just Got Smarter.

This is one of the most exciting improvements in the September update, and for blind podcast listeners we believe it could be one of the most useful.

Think about listening to a podcast which lasts an hour or more. Perhaps it begins with an introduction, moves on to the news, contains two or three interviews, includes a product demonstration or review, answers listener questions and finally ends with some closing comments. If you want to return to one particular part, how do you find it?

For a sighted listener, the podcast application may offer visual clues. There may be a progress bar, artwork, headings, visible show notes or other information on screen which helps to give some sense of where they are in the programme. For a blind person listening with a screen reader, an hour-long podcast can all too easily feel like one continuous piece of audio. You can move backwards and forwards, certainly, but you may have very little idea where the part you want actually begins.

Chapter marks change that completely.

When a podcast contains chapters, Leasey can present the programme almost as though it were a document containing headings. Instead of thinking, “The interview I want was somewhere around 35 minutes into this programme”, you can move through meaningful sections such as Introduction, News Round-Up, Interview with John Smith, Product Review, Listener Questions and Closing Comments. That is what Leasey offers at the moment. You can explore the structure of the programme and go directly to the section which interests you, either by bringing up a list of chapter marks or navigating through them sequentially.

For a blind listener, that is not simply a convenience. It gives long-form audio something it has traditionally lacked: structure which can be navigated.

We have therefore been astonished to discover just how few podcasts actually contain chapter information. Some excellent programmes lasting an hour, two hours or even longer provide no chapters at all. If the podcast producer has not created them, ordinarily there is nothing a podcast player can do about it.

Until now.

If an episode does not contain its own chapter marks, Leasey can offer to create suggested chapters for you.

Leasey can identify significant changes of subject and suggest appropriate divisions in the programme. It can then turn those divisions into chapter marks which you can use while listening.

Imagine a two-hour technology podcast with no chapters. Rather than repeatedly jumping forward and listening for clues, Leasey may be able to identify sections covering Windows, JAWS, smartphones, artificial intelligence, listener questions and so on. You can then move through those suggested chapters until you find the subject you want.

It is important to understand that these automatically created chapters are suggestions. Leasey is examining the podcast and making its best judgement about where one section ends and another begins. The podcast producer has not supplied those divisions, and Leasey cannot guarantee that every suggested chapter title or starting point will be perfect.

But perfection is not really the point. Without chapter information, you may have a 90-minute recording containing no navigational structure whatsoever. If Leasey can turn that into eight or ten sensibly named sections which allow you to move quickly around the programme, the difference can be enormous.

For many years, blind people have become accustomed to navigating written information by headings, links, lists and other structural elements. We think long-form audio deserves the same kind of attention. With podcast chapter marks, Leasey is attempting to provide exactly that: turning a long stretch of audio into something you can explore, navigate and return to with far greater independence.

Recently Heard Radio Stations.

Radio has also gained several improvements.

Leasey Media Centre now keeps a list of recently heard radio stations. This is different from the existing Most Recent button or keystroke, which plays only the last station heard.

The new recent stations list lets you review stations you have played recently, choose one and play it again. You can also add a station from that list to Favourites if you decide you want to keep it permanently.

This is a very practical addition. Many of us find stations casually. We try something, move on, and later cannot remember exactly what it was called. The recent stations list gives you a way back.

Radio Song History.

Some radio stations send song title and artist information while they are playing. When that information is available, Leasey Media Centre can now keep a song history list.

This means that if you hear a song you like, you do not necessarily need to stop what you are doing to write it down. Later, you can open the song history and review what was played. But this isn’t a regular Song History feature. It goes a great deal further than that.

You can copy song details to the clipboard.

You can also ask Leasey to tell you more about the song using the ChatGPT API key stored in Leasey’s settings. When information is available, this can include an overview, genre, notable elements, context, chart performance, artist trivia, cultural impact, behind-the-scenes information and concluding notes.

For music lovers, this is one of those features which may quickly become addictive.

Player Information.

Leasey Media Player now includes a reviewable information window for the current item.

This can include the title, podcast name, current playback position, total duration, time remaining, playback speed, whether the item is streaming or local, whether a podcast episode has been saved permanently, bookmark information and whether automatic resume playback is enabled.

The information is displayed in an edit field so it can be reviewed with standard JAWS reading commands.

This is another example of giving the user control. It is one thing to hear a short spoken status message. It is another to have information in a reviewable form so you can read it carefully.

Audio Notes.

Audio Notes allow you to attach notes to positions in local audio files or podcast temporary playback copies.

This can be useful in many situations.

You might be listening to a lecture and want to mark an important explanation.

You might be reviewing a meeting recording and want to note an action point.

You might be studying an audio course and want to remind yourself that a particular section needs revisiting.

You might be listening to a podcast and want to capture a thought before it disappears.

Leasey can also announce when audio notes are available during playback, if you choose to enable that option.

Copying One Section of an Audio File to Another.

Leasey Media Player can now copy a useful section of one local audio file to another. After all, you can easily do this with text, so why not audio?

You mark the beginning of the section, mark the end, preview it, and then save that selection as a new file. The original file is not changed.

This is useful for extracting a clip from a longer recording, saving a demonstration, keeping a short extract from a lecture, or preparing an audio example.

Again, the feature has been designed with a clear workflow:

  • Mark the start.
  • Mark the end.
  • Preview the selection.
  • Save it if you are happy. You can also append further segments of audio if you wish, either to the same file or an alternative one.

What Comes Next?

Leasey Texts and Leasey Media Centre are only part of the September update. In the second post, we will look at new improvements to LeaseySocial, Talk to ChatGPT, LeaseyWord, Leasey Spell Check and Leasey File Manager.

The update is planned for release on 1 September 2026.

What’s New in Leasey 11.5: The September Update, Part 2

Release date: 1 September 2026.

In the first post about the September update, we looked at the rewritten Leasey Texts application, the new Clipboard History feature and the many improvements to Leasey Media Centre.

This second post continues the tour.

As before, this is not a complete list of every change. The documentation will provide that level of detail. After the release date, you are strongly encouraged to review the documentation, even for areas of Leasey you think you know well. For example, not everything was covered in the previous blog post about Leasey Media Centre, such as:

  • If you are a producer of a podcast, Leasey can help you create chapter marks which can form part of the file metadata for distribution to other podcast clients supporting chapter navigation. This is huge for people who previously had no idea how to do this.
  • Special accommodation is made for playback of audio books.
  • Leasey can remember the volume level for individual items, such as radio stations or other audio files. This is not an automatic process; that is by design. So you do need to thoroughly review that chapter of the documentation again. As usual, very careful explanations have been given to work through all tasks.

The September update continues the same theme as the original 11.5 release: take features people are using every day, listen carefully, and make them faster, clearer and more comfortable.

LeaseySocial: Still Moving Forward.

LeaseySocial was one of the largest new features in Leasey 11.5. It provides a fast, keyboard-driven, JAWS-friendly Windows client for Mastodon and Bluesky, with speech, Braille, sounds, global hotkeys and extensive customisation at the heart of the design.

The September update adds several new capabilities and refinements.

Quick Navigation Keys.

LeaseySocial already has many shortcut keys, menu commands and context menu actions. However, when you are reading social media quickly, sometimes even a full shortcut key can feel like one step too many.

Quick Navigation Keys provide single-letter commands while focus is in the Posts list.

They are switched on or off with JAWS Key+Z, and they are off by default. That is an important design decision. We do not want letters typed in the Posts list to perform actions unless the user has deliberately enabled the feature.

When Quick Navigation Keys are on, you can use single letters for common tasks.

For example:

  • N creates a new post.
  • R replies to the author.
  • A replies to all relevant users.
  • D opens a direct message.
  • F favourites or unfavourites the focused post.
  • B boosts or removes a boost.
  • K bookmarks or removes a bookmark.
  • G opens the conversation.
  • Q quotes a post.
  • E translates a post to or from another language.
  • O opens a web page.
  • T invokes ChatGPT Tools.
  • C speaks the context for a reply where available.
  • P opens the profile.
  • U opens a user timeline.
  • Y speaks relationship information.
  • 1 through to 9 switch to timelines one through to nine, and 0 switches to timeline ten.
  • Escape closes the current temporary or custom timeline. For people who live in social media, this could make a big difference. It allows reading and acting to become extremely fluid. Move through posts, press one letter to reply, another to bookmark, another to open a conversation, another to look at a profile. It reduces the amount of key holding and makes LeaseySocial feel even more like a purpose-built application rather than a web page wrapped in extra commands.

Following Hashtags.

Mastodon users often use hashtags to follow events, conferences, communities, topics or breaking discussions. In the September update, LeaseySocial can follow a hashtag.

Following a hashtag asks Mastodon to place posts containing that hashtag into your Home timeline. This may include posts from people you do not follow, which is precisely why the feature is useful.

For example, if there is a conference hashtag, a campaign hashtag, a technology topic or a community discussion you want to monitor, you can follow it and have those posts appear naturally in your Home timeline.

You can follow a hashtag when you already know its name. You can type it with or without the number sign.

You can also follow or unfollow a hashtag from a hashtag result, such as Trending Hashtags, Followed Hashtags or hashtag search results.

This is another example of LeaseySocial trying to keep important Mastodon features inside the app, rather than forcing users to go back to the web interface for routine account management.

Queued Posts and the Outbox.

Most of the time, when you send a post, reply, quote or direct message, LeaseySocial sends it immediately.

But social media servers are not perfect. Mastodon servers can temporarily refuse requests if too many API calls have been made in a short period. This is called rate limiting. It can happen more often if someone uses several timelines, lists, hashtags, instance timelines or accounts, because the app is asking the server for more information.

There can also be temporary network problems or server errors.

In previous circumstances, a user might write a post, attempt to send it, and receive an error. That is frustrating, especially if the post is important.

The September update introduces queued posts and the Outbox.

If LeaseySocial tries to send a post and the server says it is temporarily limiting requests, the app can place the post in the Outbox. The same can happen for temporary network problems or temporary server errors.

JAWS will tell you:

Post queued and will be retried automatically.

That means the post has not yet been sent, but it has not been lost. It is waiting in the Outbox until LeaseySocial can try again.

This is not used for errors which are unlikely to succeed later. For example, if the account is not authorised, the post is not allowed, the original post cannot be found or the post text is not accepted by the server, LeaseySocial gives the normal error message instead.

The Outbox can be opened from the Tools menu or from Leasey Command Centre. You can review queued posts, hear whether they are queued or failed, hear a preview of the post and find out how many attempts have been made.

You can also edit a queued post. The edit dialog allows changes to the post text, visibility, content warning and alternative text for attached media. When you save the changes, the post remains in the Outbox and will be retried later.

This is the kind of feature you may not think about when everything is working, but you will be very glad to have it when a server is busy or a connection is unreliable.

Exclude Boosts from a User.

The profile dialog in LeaseySocial has also gained a useful Mastodon option.

For Mastodon profiles, the dialog may include a check box to exclude boosts from that user. This is available when you are following the user and the server provides the setting.

When checked, Mastodon is asked not to place that user’s boosts in your Home timeline. You still follow the user, and their own posts can still appear.

We hope this is a thoughtful feature because it reflects how people actually use social media. You may value someone’s own posts but not want every item they boost. LeaseySocial now gives access to that preference from inside the profile dialog.

Translation in LeaseySocial.

The Translate Text feature described below for LeaseyWord is also available in LeaseySocial.

It can translate selected text, or a post. It can be used with incoming or outgoing material.

That means you might translate a post someone else has written, or translate text you are preparing to send. For people who communicate across languages, this could be a very practical addition.

Focus on the Last Used Timeline.

There is a new option in LeaseySocial’s General Options:

Set focus to posts in last used timeline on startup.

When checked, LeaseySocial starts with focus in the Posts list for the timeline you were using last, if posts are available. LeaseySocial also briefly announces the timeline name, such as Home, Mentions or United View, so you know where you are. This means you can get straight onto browsing through posts and catching up on what everyone has to say.

When unchecked, LeaseySocial starts in the normal account and timeline area, which is the behaviour users have now.

This gives users a choice.

Some people want the most predictable startup position and prefer to begin at the account list. Others open LeaseySocial because they want to start reading immediately. The new option supports both styles.

Talk to ChatGPT Becomes a Real Conversation.

Talk to ChatGPT was introduced in Leasey 11.5, but the September update changes the feel of it significantly.

Previously, the process was more like recording a spoken prompt. You recorded the prompt, it was sent to ChatGPT, there was a pause while it was processed, and then the response came back.

That was useful, but it was not quite conversational.

The new version is much closer to speaking with someone. Responses are typically received within five seconds.

You start a live conversation. JAWS says:

Connecting.

When the conversation is ready, JAWS says:

Start talking.

You then speak your question naturally. When you stop speaking, Leasey detects the end of your speech and sends the question to ChatGPT. You do not need to press a key after every question.

When ChatGPT has finished answering, you can simply ask another question.

If current information is needed, Leasey may search the web, and JAWS will say:

Searching web.

If you want to stop the spoken answer and ask something else, press Alt+S. JAWS says:

Start talking.

You can then speak the next question.

This makes the feature feel much more immediate.

You might ask about the weather, then ask whether you should take a coat.

You might ask for lunch ideas, then ask for a shopping list.

You might ask for a short message cancelling an appointment, then ask for it to be warmer and shorter.

You might ask for a plain English explanation of a news item, then ask a follow-up question without repeating the background.

The transcript remains available in an edit field, and it can be copied to the clipboard if you want to keep the conversation or paste it into another document, email message or Leasey feature.

LeaseyWord: Headings, Links and Translation.

LeaseyWord continues to develop as a practical reading and writing environment.

In the September update, two small but very useful navigation commands have been added.

JAWS users will be familiar with the web commands for listing headings and links. LeaseyWord now provides similar commands for the current document.

JAWS Key+F6 opens the list of headings.

JAWS Key+F7 opens the list of links.

The headings dialog shows each heading followed by its level. You can move through the headings with Up and Down Arrow and press Enter to move to the selected heading.

The links dialog lists Markdown links, HTML links, visible web addresses and visible email addresses found in the current document. If a link has visible text and a destination, both are shown. Again, use Up and Down Arrow to move through the list and press Enter to move to the selected link.

These are not dramatic commands, but they are exactly the kind of commands that make document review faster. If you are reading a long Markdown file, HTML file, documentation chapter or converted document, being able to list headings and links immediately gives you structure.

Translate Text.

LeaseyWord also gains Translate Text. This uses ChatGPT to translate text directly inside LeaseyWord.

If text is selected, only the selected text is translated. If no text is selected, the whole document is translated.

You choose the target language from a combo box. The list includes languages such as English, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Brazilian Portuguese, Dutch, Swedish, Norwegian, Danish, Polish, Ukrainian, Welsh, Irish, Japanese and Chinese. You can also type another language if it is not in the list.

ChatGPT detects the source language automatically.

When the translation is complete, the translated text replaces the selected text. If no text was selected, it replaces the document text.

This could be useful in many situations:

  • Translating a paragraph from an email.
  • Translating a short article.
  • Preparing text for someone who reads another language.
  • Checking the meaning of a foreign-language quotation.
  • Working with multilingual social media content before sending it to LeaseySocial.

Leasey Spell Check: No More Clipboard Round Trip.

Leasey Spell Check was introduced in Leasey 11.5 to give JAWS users a consistent way of checking spelling in plain text, regardless of which application was used to write the text.

The September update improves the workflow.

Previously, spell checking involved the clipboard. Now you select the text you want to check, launch Leasey Spell Check, make corrections, and the corrected text replaces the selected text.

That is a much cleaner process.

It is especially useful in web forms, email messages, social media posts, chat windows and text editors where the built-in spell checker may not be comfortable to use with JAWS.

The spell checker still gives you the same careful review. It reports the misspelled word, spells it, provides suggestions, spells the first suggestion, allows you to change, change all, ignore, ignore all, add to the dictionary, hear the sentence again, finish or cancel.

But the important practical improvement is that you no longer need to copy text to the clipboard, run the check, return to the original application and paste the corrected version yourself. Leasey can replace the selected text directly.

Leasey Diary: Importing Holidays.

Leasey Diary has also gained a very useful new feature: it can retrieve holidays for a selected country and year, and then let you import only the ones you want.

This is exactly the kind of feature which sounds small until you need it.

Suppose you want United Kingdom public holidays in your diary for 2027. You may not want every religious observance, every local observance, or every non-public holiday. You may simply want the main public holidays so that you can plan appointments, training courses, support calls, travel arrangements or personal events without having to enter each date manually.

Leasey Diary now lets you do that in a controlled way.

You choose the year.

You choose the country.

You decide whether to include public holidays, religious holidays and non-public holidays.

Leasey retrieves the results and then shows each holiday as an individual check box. Each item includes the name, date and type of holiday. For example:

Holiday: New Year's Day, Friday 1 January 2027, Public holiday

You can then uncheck anything you do not want. If everything is suitable, you can select all. If you want to start again with nothing selected, you can clear all. When you are satisfied, you import the selected holidays.

Imported holidays are created as all-day appointments. They do not set reminders. They are also marked so that they do not take part in conflict warnings. Their subjects begin with the word Holiday, making them easy to recognise in the diary.

Leasey also tries to avoid creating duplicates. If it finds that a holiday already exists on the same date with the same subject, it skips that item rather than creating another copy.

This feature should be particularly useful at the beginning of a new year, when setting up a diary for work, training, personal planning or shared family arrangements. It gives you the convenience of importing holidays without forcing you to accept every item returned.

Conclusion.

Together with the rewritten Leasey Texts, new Clipboard History and the Media Centre improvements described in the first post, this is a substantial update shaped entirely by user feedback.

The update is planned for release on 1 September 2026. Some of the new features will be demonstrated during the Accessible World Tek Talk event for 31 August 2026. This is particularly appropriate because they were the first group of people ever to see Leasey in action prior to the release of version 1.

We are grateful to everyone who has helped test, question, challenge and improve Leasey 11.5. Please keep the feedback coming. It is making a real difference.

WordWeb

WordWeb.

WordWeb is a dictionary which can be downloaded to the computer. The program has a full dictionary and thesaurus for American, British, Canadian, Australian, Indian, and global English. The WordWeb program does not form part of the Leasey installer, but it can be downloaded at no cost from the organisation’s website. Leasey ensures that the program is very accessible.

WordWeb can be launched by selecting it from the Windows Start Menu in the same way that you would launch any other Windows program. Note that in WordWeb’s Settings dialog, (activated by pressing ALT+O then P), an option exists to start WordWeb when Windows is launched, if you wish to activate it.

One way of using WordWeb is as follows:

  • Find a word for which you wish to know its meaning. This can be done from within any application.

  • Copy it to the Windows Clipboard by selecting it first and then pressing Control+C. Note that in many cases, selecting the text is sufficient. However, JAWS often presents text in a virtual environment, such as when browsing web pages. Therefore, the safest option is to copy it to the Windows Clipboard.

  • When copied, press the shortcut key for WordWeb, ALT+Control+W. This brings the WordWeb program into focus and the first definition will be announced automatically now Leasey has been installed.

  • Press the Down Arrow key repeatedly to work through all the definitions for the word. These will be announced.

  • You do have the option of pressing the Tab key to move through the choices. JAWS has been scripted so as to read all the information, including the series of tabbed pages available. For example, if you press the Tab key to readh the Tabbed Pages, you may find the Synonyms Tab, the Antonyms Tab, and so on.

  • When any Tabbed Page is selected, press the Tab key once more to focus on a list of words relative to the Tabbed Page which are associated with the original word.

  • Use the Up or Down Arrow key to move through the list. When you reach the desired word, press Enter, and again you will be automatically focused in the list of definitions. You may like to work through the following example:

  • In a document, type the word, “ridiculous”.

  • Select the word so it is highlighted, and then copy it to the Clipboard with Control+C.

  • Press ALT+Control+W so as to launch WordWeb.

  • The list of definitions is available. Use the Up and Down Arrow keys to move through (and hear) them.

  • Press the Tab key. You will note you are focused on the Synonyms Tab. You can if necessary press Tab once more to focus upon a list of Synonyms.

  • Press Enter on a word to review the definitions for that word.

  • Alternatively, while on the series of Tabbed Pages, press Right Arrow. You will find that focus is now on the Antonyms Tab.

  • If you wish, press Tab to move into this Tabbed Page. As before, locate the desired word with the Arrow keys and press Enter to explore the definitions.

  • To close the WordWeb window, press ALT+F4. This does not exit WordWeb. You can repeat the above procedure at any time by copying a word to the Clipboard and pressing ALT+Control+W so as to browse definitions. Back to Help Index.

Working with Email, for Leasey Basic and Advanced Users

Working with Email, for Leasey Basic and Advanced Users.

Microsoft Outlook Classic.

There are a number of useful utilities for those who are using both Leasey packages.

If you are inside an Email message, and you wish to copy the sender’s Email address to the Windows Clipboard, press the Leasey Key then Control+Shift+E. The Email address will be spoken back to you for confirmation and it is now copied to the Clipboard ready for pasting elsewhere.

Another component of Microsoft Outlook email relates to sending a message from an alternative account. Use this method in order to verify which account you are sending from:

  • Press ALT+M from within the body of the Email message in order to set focus to the list of accounts.
  • Press Down Arrow to select the account in question.
  • Press Enter.
  • Focus back on the body of the Email message.
  • Press the Leasey Key then Control+Shift+A. You should hear the account details spoken to you. Leasey has the ability to place all attachments into a vertical list for easy navigation and opening. This is especially helpful for two reasons. First, many people find it easier to work with vertical lists, so that the Up and Down Arrow keys can be used. However in addition, if people insert an attachment into the body of an Email message, this is often rendered as a graphic rather than appearing in the default Microsoft Outlook Attachments area. The Leasey Attachments List keystroke provides access to all attachments regardless of their type.

To view all attachments in a message, from within the message body press ALT+Windows+A. The list of attachments appears.

Use the Up or Down Arrow keys to move to the attachment you wish to open, then press Enter.

If you wish to copy an attachment to an alternative location, follow these steps:

  • Locate the attachment from the aforementioned list but do not press Enter in order to open it.
  • Press Shift+Tab to reach the “Copy” Button and press Enter or the Space Bar.
  • Using File Explorer, browse to the folder in which you wish to place the attached file.
  • Press Control+V to paste the attached file into the chosen location. If you receive an Email containing an MP3 audio file as an attachment, be sure the message is open and press ALT+Windows+U. The file will play out using your default audio player.

When focused in an Email folder, it is easy to flag items for later review. This means you can create a copy of them to add to your “To-Do List”, meaning that you can always get back to them to follow up later.

  • Find a message you wish to flag.

  • Press Control+Windows+F.

  • The email is added to your “To-Do List”.

  • Repeat this process until all messages for follow-up have been flagged.

  • When appropriate, press Control+4 to move to the “To-Do List”.

  • When inside this list, you can manage your email messages in whichever way you choose: Open them, reply to them, etc.

  • To unflag a message, press Control+Windows+F once again. Note that whenever you press this keystroke, JAWS reports whether the message is flagged for review or not.

  • To return to your mail folder at any time from your “To-Do List”, press Control+1. You can use the keystroke Control+Shift+Enter to set focus to the Results List when Outlook Search is used. Here is an example of how you might work with this process.

  • From within a mail folder, press Control+E.

  • Type a word or phrase you wish to find in the folder. After a short pause, the results view changes to display only messages matching your search criteria.

  • Press Control+Shift+Enter. Leasey will set focus to the list of results. This saves a good deal of navigating around with either F6 or the Tab key. You can now go ahead and explore the results by using the Up or Down Arrow keys.

Suppressing The From Field From Being Spoken When Messages Are Open.

Unless disabled from within the JAWS Quick Settings, (JAWS Key+V), as a message is opened JAWS will read who the message is from, followed by the word “Subject”, then the subject line. This can seriously decrease productivity, since there is a distinct possibility you are already aware of the original author.

If you wish to hear the subject line only, press ALT+Windows+F from within Outlook. This is a toggle action and will ensure the feature is either on or off. If enabled, JAWS will only read the subject line when focus moves to a new message.

Automatic Speaking of the Outlook Reading Pane.

Through Leasey, JAWS has the ability to automatically speak the content of the Outlook reading pane as you move through messages in a mail folder. This means that if the reading pane is enabled, as you move to a new message JAWS will speak the usual details such as the presence of attachments, author and subject, followed by the content of the reading pane. In most cases, the reading pane displays the entire content of a message. This can be very helpful because you can read your Email messages without opening them. Listening to this information can help in making a decision as to whether you wish to open the message, move it elsewhere or delete it.

Setting It Up.

There are a number of steps in terms of customising whether the reading pane is displayed and whether it is announced by JAWS.

First, focus within the Outlook application and enable the automatic reading of the reading pane by pressing the Leasey key then Control+Shift+R. This is a toggle action and will enable and disable the feature. The setting is remembered even if you restart JAWS. In terms of the next two tasks, the procedures for working through these may vary between different versions of Microsoft Office. The reading pane is enabled by default, so it may be there is very little to do following enabling JAWS to read it automatically which we have already done. If you move through a mail folder and JAWS is speaking the contents of the reading pane, you can leave things as they are. If the reading pane is not enabled:

  • Activate the “View” component of the ribbon with ALT+V.
  • Press the Tab key repeatedly until you move into the “Layout” group. Eventually JAWS will announce “Reading Pane”. Press Enter. Alternatively, press ALT+V then P then N.
  • Press Down Arrow until JAWS announces “Bottom” or “Right”. These terms indicate the position of the reading pane on the screen; either at the bottom or on the righthand side.
  • Press Enter on any one of these two options. If JAWS is announcing that one of these is checked, such as “Bottom Checked”, then it is already being displayed and you can press Escape to close the menu. To aid productivity, there is a further adjustment you may like to make.

You will probably want to remove the columns in the mail folder view which display the date and size of the message. Not hearing this information will mean that your message details can be spoken without unwanted text, followed by the reading pane content.

  • Activate the “View” component of the ribbon with ALT+V.
  • Press the Tab key repeatedly until you move into the “Arrangement” group. Eventually JAWS will announce “Add Columns”. Despite its name, this is where you want to be. Press Enter. Alternatively, press ALT+V then A then C. Think Vacation!
  • This is a dialog box allowing you to modify which columns are displayed. Press the Tab key until JAWS announces “Show columns, show columns in this order”. This is a list box. It is the control which immediately preceeds the “OK” button in the Tab order.
  • Press Down Arrow until JAWS announces “Received” and then press ALT+R to remove it.
  • Press Down Arrow until JAWS announces “Size” and then press ALT+R to remove it.
  • Press Tab until you reach “OK” and press the Space Bar.
Mozilla Thunderbird.

A small number of enhancements have been provided for use within Mozilla Thunderbird. Microsoft Outlook Classic is still the recommended option for efficient Email management.

The following keys can be press from within an Email message.

  • ALT+Windows+1 through to ALT+Windows+5 will read header information in relation to the message which is open. For example, ALT+Windows+1 will read who the message is from. ALT+Windows+2 will read the date of the message.
  • Pressing the Leasey key then Control+Shift+E will copy the sender’s Email address to the Windows Clipboard.
Automatic Message Reading.

JAWS provides an option within Quick Settings so as to read Email messages automatically when they are opened by pressing Enter. Leasey will eliminate unimportant speech and skip the first line, which is always a repetition of the subject.

To enable automatic reading:

  • With Thunderbird open, press JAWS Key+V.
  • Into the Search Edit Field, type the phrase, “Auto Read”.
  • Arrow down and you will find the only result returned: Auto Read Message.
  • If it is not checked, press Space Bar to check it.
  • Press Enter twice to save.
Moving to Core Thunderbird Components.

Pressing Control+Comma will set focus to Thunderbird Preferences.

ALT+Windows+L will move to the next available list, such as a list of messages in a mail folder.

ALT+Windows+T will move to the next Tree View, such as a list of folders.

Setting the Default Inbox.

Thunderbird does not provide a mechanism to launch the Inbox for a specific mail account when the program starts. To achieve this, please work through the following process:

  • Be sure that the focus is located on the Inbox name. You will find this in the list of folders, such as Inbox, Sent Items, etc.
  • When focus is on the Inbox, press ALT+Windows+D.
  • After a short pause, a shortcut should be placed on the Windows Desktop. The Shortcut is called, Leasey Thunderbird. You can always rename it if you like by pressing function key F2, however the shortcut itself must remain intact.
Spell Checking.

When spell checking an Email message, you can press ALT+Windows+I. This will speak and spell the incorrectly spelled word. Back to Help Index.

Working with Email, for Leasey Basic Users

Working with Email, for Leasey Basic Users.

Working with Email in the most part is self-explanatory. When you launch the item on the Leasey Main Menu, �Check Your Email�, the Email client you have chosen through LeaseyManager will launch.

A Leasey Application Menu is available for most common email tasks. However, this menu is different depending upon the task you are working through. For example, the menu of choices activated when you are in the list of messages received is different to the one for when a message is being composed. Back to Help Index.

Working with Leasey and JAWS 2026

Introduction.

JAWS version 2026 is now available. This blog post gives useful information about upgrading to this new version and how to install Leasey into it in the correct way.

Should I Upgrade JAWS to version 2026?

Certainly yes. It is my view that this version is a significant improvement over 2025 in many areas and you are strongly advised to upgrade to it. If you have not paid for an upgrade to JAWS 2026 yet, or you do not have a Software Maintenance Agreement, you seriously want to think about this fairly quickly.

Should I Uninstall JAWS Version 2025 or 2024?

Absolutely not. I heard a podcast recently which suggested doing this. This is not recommended. When I install a new version of JAWS for any customer, I always keep a previous version installed.

Why is that? Because if the new release of JAWS does not work well with an application you use regularly, or there are difficulties with customising specific settings, you have a version you can go back to. JAWS versions can coexist on the same machine and you may wish to return to an earlier version. This is good advice you are being given.

Please do not uninstall the previous version until you are 100 percent satisfied that the new release is doing exactly what you want.

This advice also applies in the workplace; indeed it is even more important there.

How to Install Leasey Into JAWS 2026.

Thanks to Vispero, a number of our Leasey Beta Testers were able to test the product with JAWS 2026, so we know the below procedure is correct.

Installing JAWS 2026.

Please work through the following procedure.

  • If you live in the United States, you are required to create an account to use JAWS version 2026. It is suggested that you do this as a first step. Visit this page to do so.
  • Download and launch the JAWS 2026 application from the Vispero web site. If you are offered this upgrade as part of the automatic JAWS update process, the below instructions equally apply.
  • Within the initial screen of the JAWS installation procedure, there are two Check boxes. The first, which is immediately in focus, prompts you to accept the License Agreement. There is an opportunity to read this which you may care to do. Assuming you agree with its terms, press the Space Bar to check it.
  • This next step is critical. Press the Tab key to reach the next Check Box. This offers to migrate your settings from a previous version to the new one. Press the Space Bar to uncheck this box. If Leasey is installed, this merge procedure fails. We will merge settings in a later step.
  • You can now press Enter to proceed with the installation as usual and restart the computer when prompted. You can then sign in with your account if prompted to do so.
Installing Leasey into JAWS 2026.

Please work through the following procedure.

  • Download and install Leasey from the Hartgen Consultancy web site. This must be Leasey build 1080 or above. Please do not install any other Leasey build if it is below 1080. The link pointing to the download always states the build number.
  • Note that since February of this year, the company web site URL has changed. This has been heavily promoted since then. You can Download Leasey here.
  • Launch the program you have just downloaded. In most cases, pressing Enter to activate the “Next” Button on each screen should be sufficient. Following the opening screen, you will be asked to accept the Licence Agreement. Press the Tab key to reach a group of Radio buttons, any one of which can be selected by pressing the Up or Down Arrow keys. You should select the Radio button so as to accept the Licence Agreement, then press Enter to proceed. If you wish, you can read the Licence Agreement by pressing the Tab key so as to reach its Edit Field, and then work through it in the usual manner for reading text.
  • On the next screen, the Leasey installer detects the versions of JAWS which are installed onto the machine and presents you with a series of Radio Buttons, inviting you to choose which release you would like to install Leasey into. JAWS 2026 is the most recent version so that should be the default. If necessary, press the Down Arrow key to select the version of JAWS you wish to use,, then press Enter.
  • You will next be asked for a language folder into which Leasey should be installed. This refers to the JAWS language settings to be used. You should press the Down Arrow key until “enu (English US)” is selected, then press Enter. Indeed, this is usually the first item in the list.
  • If you are installing Leasey into JAWS 2026, you will next be asked if you would like to import your existing settings from JAWS 2024 or 2025. There are three options in the Combo Box: Do not import, import from JAWS 2024 or import from JAWS 2025. If you do choose to import from JAWS 2024 or 2025, this includes any JAWS configuration files, voice profiles and notification rules you may have available in the older JAWS version. JAWS 2025 is the default option. If this is not to your taste, press Down Arrow to select one of the other options and then press Enter.
  • Prior to copying the necessary files to the computer, you will be asked to confirm the location of the installation of JAWS script files. If JAWS is being used by a person with an alternative Windows account to the one shown, you should correct this in the Edit Field before proceeding, changing the text so it points to the Leasey user’s account instead. The majority of users will not have to be at all concerned with this screen and can just press Enter to continue with the Leasey installation. For I T Administrators in a corporate environment however, (who may be logged onto the computer using a different account to that of the user), this will be particularly important.
  • Finally, prior to the installation proceeding, the installer will make a copy of your existing JAWS settings. These are located at c:XXX Backup, where XXX is the JAWS version number. The reason a folder is created with the JAWS version number is that if you decide to install Leasey into multiple JAWS versions, your original settings from that release can be reinstated if necessary. A Dialog Box will be displayed, stating the exact backup path. Press Enter to proceed.
  • When the installer has completed creating the additional folders required for Leasey, and copying files to them, you will be prompted to restart the computer and you should comply with this request. This is critical! At that point, if you have chosen to import settings from a previous JAWS version, they should now be active together with the most current version of Leasey.
What Happens If The Above Advice for Installing JAWS and Leasey Has Been Ignored?

You may be in a position where someone has installed JAWS for you and did not uncheck the Migrate Settings Check Box. In such a situation, running the Leasey installer and choosing to import settings from a previous version of JAWS should resolve most problems. However, the cleanest way of resolving the situation is as follows:

  • With JAWS 2026 running, press Insert+J to move to the JAWS window.
  • Select “Options”.
  • Select “Restore to Factory Settings”.
  • You are asked if you would like to go ahead. Select “Yes”.
  • JAWS will restart in its default configuration. You can then run the Leasey installer and proceed with the steps above.

Conclusion.

Do enjoy using Leasey with JAWS 2026. We know it is going to be an excellent experience. If you feel you would prefer some assistance with installing Leasey into this new version, remote assistance is available assuming you have Remote Incident Manager installed. If you haven’t got it installed, why not? Everyone should have it. You can download it here.

Working With Sounds

Working With Sounds.

This brief section of the documentation will discuss the Leasey Sounds Scheme.

Why are Sounds Used?

There are a number of events which occur that are specific to Leasey. These are events such as when a web page has completed loading and is ready for use, when you begin and end the selecting of text, to denote the use of LeaseyPoints and LeaseyClips, to name but a few items. The use of all of these tools will be discussed in later sections of this document. But in essence, switching to the Leasey Sound Scheme will ensure you can work faster, particularly with tools such as LeaseyClips. The sound earcons are quicker to hear and interpret rather than a long block of speech being spoken.

By default Leasey events are announced through speech by the software, but there are two other options available to you. You can elect to have Sounds alone played, have Leasey only announce events, or have both. Sounds with speech is a very good way to learn what the various Sounds mean. The setting for Leasey Sounds can be found and manipulated by pressing the Leasey Key followed by letter “O”. Each time you press this keystroke, you will rotate between the three available options: Sounds Off, Sounds On and Sounds with Speech. Back to Help Index.

Working with the Internet, for Leasey Advanced Users

Working with the Internet, for Leasey Advanced Users.

If you are a Leasey Advanced user only, JAWS will interpret web pages in the usual way and all the navigation keys are available. However, there are some additional tools you may like to take advantage of, described elsewhere in this document, including:

  • LeaseySelect;
  • LeaseyPoints;
  • LeaseyCuts;
  • LeaseySticky Notes;
  • LeaseyFavourites;
  • LeaseyAlerts. Google Chrome, Firefox, Brave or Microsoft Edge Chromium browsers are supported for use with Leasey.

You will notice that, if sounds are enabled, a tone will play when a new page is loaded and a “backwards” sound can be heard when you move back to a previous page.

Pressing full-stop (or period) by itself will move to the next link irrespective of its type, whether it has been visited or unvisited.

Pressing Comma by itself will move to the previous link irrespective of its type, whether it has been visited or unvisited.

If you are using Microsoft Edge, you may come across situations where JAWS is advising you of the status of page activity, such as “Loading Page”. Some people find this very helpful while others do not. Leasey attempts to suppress some of these messages from being spoken. To attempt to stop such messages from being spoken, press Control+Shift+A while within Microsoft Edge. This is a toggle keystroke to enable and disable such messages. This is only applicable to JAWS versions earlier than 2022. In version 2022, Vispero have a feature available called Notification History where you can control such spoken or Braille-based output.

Note that it is possible to remove some of the messages which are being filtered so they will be spoken. For example, if you would like the majority of messages emanating from Microsoft Edge to be filtered, with the exception of the phrase “Going Back”, you can cherry-pick the ones you want.

In the following folder, there is a file called Edge.TXT. c:

Simply open up that file and remove the messages to avoid them being filtered, in our example, Going back. Similarly, if Microsoft introduce additional messages which are unwanted in the future, you can add these to the text file.

Most people however will want to leave this file intact.

You may also encounter a situation as follows. If you activate a link on a web site by pressing Enter so as to reveal a new page, then press ALT+Left Arrow so as to return to the previous page, JAWS may not remember the position where the Virtual Cursor was previously located. To attempt to relocate your previous position on the page, press the Leasey key then Control+Shift+R. You can apply this function automatically by pressing ALT+Windows+R which will enable or disable it. In that event, whenever you move back to a page, Leasey will attempt to more thoroughly relocate your position on the page where you left off reading.

Additional Browser Utilities.

A number of other utilities exist which require special explanation.

Storing Web Pages as Favourites.

Using Microsoft Internet Explorer, locating sites you had previously stored as Favourites was an easy process. All such shortcuts used to be placed in a special folder for the purpose, which could be located from the Windows “Start Menu”, or indeed a Shortcut could be placed on the Windows Desktop. Activating such a shortcut would take you into a list of all your Favourites which if necessary you could divide into separate sub-folders so as to group them into categories.

Unfortunately, those days are gone. If you store a site as a Favourite in a modern browser, it is accommodated within a specially constructed database which you have to work through inside the browser. Leasey takes away this frustration and provides you wit a method of storing shortcuts to Favourites either within your Favourites folder you may have previously used, or indeed any folder of your choosing.

Prior to reading through this option, we suggest you review the section of this documentation on the subject of LeaseyCuts, because the creation of LeaseyCuts is far easier than what is described here. However, old habits die hard, and it could be that you would still prefer to use the old method of working with Favourites.

Before you begin, you must instruct Leasey as to which folder contains your Favourites. So, either open up the Favourites folder you previously used, or alternatively, browse to a new one. In most cases, what you are about to do is a one time process unless you specifically want to store Favourites in a new folder at a later time. You can also store favourites in subsequent folders if you wish, which will be described below, however this is an optional step.

Now, press ALT+L. The location is stored permanently unless you change it.

  • Using Brave, Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge, browse to the website you wish to store as a Favourite.
  • Press ALT+A. You will be asked to name the item to be stored as a Favourite. The name of the previously focused page is already displayed in the edit field. You can leave it intact, edit it or Type in a new name and press Enter. There is nothing further to do. Just browse to the folder in File Explorer, or by locating your Favourites folder, and your newly created Favourite will be there waiting for you.
Storing Favourites in Additional Folders.

It could be that you wish to save Favourites in additional folders. Let’s assume for example that you have a folder into which you wish to place web site favourites you visit for stores. You might have a separate folder for music related sites and so on.

If this is the case, please do the following.

First, browse to the new folder using File Explorer into which favourites could potentially be saved. Open it up by pressing Enter so you are inside the folder.

Press ALT+L. If you did this using the first incarnation of Leasey version 5, we suggest you go through this process again as Leasey needs to know more information about the folder.

Repeat as necessary until all your folders are set.

Now, browse to the site into which the favourite should be stored in one of your folders.

Press ALT+W. This now brings into view a list of all the folders you have set.

Arrow down until you reach the folder you wish to use, then press Enter to move to the next stage.

You should now be on familiar ground. The name of the previously focused page is already displayed in the edit field. You can leave it intact, edit it or Type in a new name and press Enter. If you open up that new folder now, you should see the shortcut in there.

Points to note. First, any favourites you save from this point forward will be placed in the newly designated folder. If you wish to go back to one of your original folders, you should press ALT+W, and set it as described earlier.

Secondly, if you would like to delete one of the folders from the list, this can be done by pressing ALT+W, finding the folder name, and pressing the Leasey Key followed by Delete. This does not in any way remove the folder from the computer. This would not be good practice. All Leasey is doing is removing the linking mechanism between Leasey and the folder itself.

Tabbed Pages.

You may know that as you are browsing web pages, you can open the focused web page in a new Tab. For example, when focused on a Link, you can open it in a new Tab by pressing Control+Enter. JAWS confirms that a new Tab has been created.

There are a number of ways by which you can navigate through the Tabbed pages. The easiest way would be to press Control+Tab or Control+Page Down to move forward through Tabs, and press Shift+Control+Tab or Control+Page Up to move in the reverse direction. You can also press Control+1 through to Control+8, using the numbers above the letter keys. This will automatically set focus to any one of the first eight Tabs in the order in which they were created.

But what if you cannot remember which Tab is associated with any one of the eight keystrokes? There are two things you can do to remind you.

  • As you navigate through Tabs, (for example with Control+Tab or Shift+Control+Tab), JAWS will indicate the Tab number.
  • Additionally, you can press the Leasey Key then Control+Shift+N, which will speak or Braille the Tab number of the focused page. Back to Help Index.

Working with the Internet, for Leasey Basic Users

Working with the Internet, for Leasey Basic Users.

When using Leasey Basic, and you launch the third item on the menu which is “Surf the Internet”, a web page will be loaded with a prompt inviting you to press the Leasey Application Menu key or Escape for options. Having done this, there are a number of choices you can make, including browsing to a new website if you know the address, moving to the search results on a website, start reading from the top of the page, and more.

We strongly recommend that users of Leasey Basic take full advantage of the DAISY training material provided, as this gives very clear background information as to the purpose of the internet, together with good strategies for navigating pages. Back to Help Index.

X With Leasey

X With Leasey.

Introduction.

X is a micro-blogging service which can be used to exchange quick frequent messages. Particularly in recent months at the time of writing, X has undergone many changes to the extent that there are now two levels of X access available. The standard usage is a free X account allowing you to compose messages of up to 280 characters in length. The second is X Premium allowing messages of up to 25 thousand characters and other features for subscribers.

For many years, a small number of specially developed applications were available to screen-reader users which made the management of X posts quick and easy. However, again due to recent changes, the majority of such X clients are no longer permitted to access the service. As far as access to X using the Windows operating system is concerned, it is therefore necessary to use either the X app from the Microsoft App Store or the web site at X.com. The access you will receive is exactly the same.

While many people would say that X itself provides a number of accessibility enhancements to allow people to use either of these methods of access, the reality is that it is not the most optimum experience. The output from the screen-reader is very verbose, since it delivers a great deal of information potentially you would not wish to hear. When using some versions of JAWS, it requires that the JAWS Virtual Cursor is disabled in order that the special shortcut keys can be used. Those shortcut keys are not particularly easy to remember. There are a number of other reasons. To this end, the X scripts provide some support so you can still access X fairly efficiently using any one of the above mentioned methods of access. The level of access is not going to be of the same high quality and efficiency as previously provided by the older specialist clients. That access is a thing of the past. But it is our hope that the assistance given here will at the very least allow you to keep up-to-date, especially with mainstream organisations who are present there. X is a thriving community of people with millions of users and it is important that you are not locked out of having quality access to it.

It is the view of Hartgen Consultancy that at the time of writing, you would not wish to use X for everyday conversation and interaction, despite the support which has been put in place here. If you are using a screen-reader with Windows, the days of doing that efficiently are gone. The purpose of what follows is to allow you to keep abreast of X activity which may be essential.

What follows is a brief summary of how you might accomplish tasks you may typically wish to work through on X. It is by no means exhaustive and improvements to this access will, if possible, be made over time.

It is also worth mentioning that this is not a tutorial on using X. It does not attempt to explain X terms. The below documentation sections summarise specifically how the X scripts can assist you in working with X and nothing more.

Let’s Get Started.

When X is launched, at least for the first time, you will want to press Insert+Q (or Caps Lock+Q if you are using the JAWS Laptop Layout). If JAWS announces that the scripts for X are loaded, you can proceed.

A Note About the JAWS Virtual Cursor.

As previously indicated, in order for you to gain a meaningful experience with X, the JAWS Virtual Cursor needs to be disabled. In terms of The JAWS scripts for X, this occurs by default. As soon as you launch X from the web site or via the official app, the Virtual Cursor is switched off and, to a large extent, you can navigate X as if it was a standard application. However, there may be times when you wish to enable it, particularly when customising settings as an example. You can do this at any time by pressing Insert+Z (or Caps Lock+Z if you are using the JAWS laptop layout). This is a toggle action and will enable and disable the feature. Once enabled, X can be accessed in the same way as you would read (and interact with) a regular web page.

X Basic Principles.

From this point forward, when X is accessed, you will probably be on your Home timeline where you will see posts from the people and organisations you follow. Press Up or Down Arrow keys to move through the posts. You will probably hear the author name, the X username, the time the post was sent, the post itself and, if appropriate, statistical information such as the number of likes.

You may find that you wish to abbreviate some of this information. To do this, activate Abbreviated Mode. This can be toggled on and off with ALT+Windows+A. Once enabled, this setting will remain in effect until you disable it. Enabling Abbreviated Mode has the effect of reducing the output so you hear all the details with the exception of the X username and the time, so it makes navigation a lot less of a chore.

Should you wish to hear all of this information, you can use the JAWS command to read the current line, Insert+Up Arrow (or Caps Lock+Up Arrow if you are using the JAWS laptop layout). Pressing this keystroke twice quickly will allow you to read all of the information in the JAWS Virtual Viewer for closer examination, perhaps word by word. Press Escape to close.

There are two ways in which posts can be displayed: using the “For You” Tab or the “Following” Tab. The “For You” Tab is the default. The advantage of the “For You” Tab is that you can meet different people who share your own interests. The more posts you reply to or like influences the X algorithm and will display items which may match your interests. Using older Twitter clients designed for visually impaired people, users were forced to only receive posts from those people being followed. This meant that an important element of social media was lost.

To change to the “Following” Tab, activate the Virtual Cursor with the JAWS Key+Z. Then, from the top of the page, arrow down until you reach the Tabs. You will find “For You” and “Following”. JAWS does announce which Tab is selected. Press the Space Bar on the appropriate Tab.

The Navigation Experience.

You will notice that your most recently received posts are at the top of the list. In the majority of cases, as you enter the X platform, the top of the list is the focus. This means that you are reading your posts in reverse time order which is not the best experience and there is no way of changing it. We cannot think of anyone who, for example, would want to start by reading the concluding part of a news story coverage and to work backwards.

Every effort has been made to ensure that, as you move through a timeline, focus does not move away from the list of posts. Should this happen, press the Tab key once, then try moving through the posts again with the down Arrow key.

There is also an added difficulty in that it does not seem possible to stop the timeline from refreshing which causes focus issues.

If you think you may have more recent posts available than those displayed, press full-stop or period to refresh the timeline.

Should you wish to access a link referenced as part of the post, press the Tab key repeatedly until JAWS announces the link. Then press Enter. The page referred to should open up as a new tab in your web browser. When you have finished reviewing the page, press Control+F4 so as to return to X.

Keystrokes you may wish to use at this point are:

  • ALT+Windows+H: Home timeline.
  • ALT+Windows+M: Mentions timeline.
  • ALT+Windows+N: Notifications timeline.
  • ALT+Windows+D: Direct Messages timeline.
  • ALT+Windows+K: Likes timeline.
  • ALT+Windows+I: Lists.
  • ALT+Windows+P: Profile.
  • ALT+Windows+S: Settings.
  • ALT+Windows+C: Change Account.
  • L: Like a post.
  • Forward Slash: Search.
  • B: Block a user.
  • Control+C, copy focused post to Clipboard. If Abbreviated Mode is enabled, only the output spoken is copied, removing the username and the time the post was posted. This is recommended.
  • U: Mute.
  • Enter: Open Post. One of the most valuable aspects of using X is being able to scan and interpret images which are frequently posted. This especially means that you can join in conversations from which you may otherwise have been excluded. This can be an essential aspect of social media participation. This can be achieved using JAWS 2024 and Picture Smart AI.

Find a post containing an image. JAWS will announce if an image is present. Then, press Control+Windows+I. The image is scanned and the text presented. You are then able to read it and, if necessary, obtain a more thorough explanation using two AI chat services and even ask further questions. For example, if a general description is given of an outfit someone is waring, you can ask for more description about it.

Press Escape to exit the description. In the event that focus is now not located on the post you were previously reading, press function key F12. The X scripts will try to locate this for you.

Post Composition.

To compose a new post, press Control+N. Start typing your text into the Edit Field. If you wish to know how many characters have been typed, press Insert+T (or Caps Lock+T if you are using the JAWS laptop layout).

To send the message, press Enter or Control+Enter.

Should you wish to attach an image (such as a photo) to the post, press ALT+Windows+P. This takes you into a standard Windows “Browse” Dialog Box. Locate the image and press Enter. Fields are then available which you can move through by pressing Tab and Shift+Tab to allow you to tag the image with alternative text.

To reply to the focused post, press Control+R.

To resend a post without quoting, press Control+Shift+R.

To Resend a post with quoting, (adding a comment), press Control+Shift+Q.

Viewing a Conversation.

There is a strong likelihood that an X post which is focused will be a reply to a previous message. This is known as being part of a conversation thread. To open up the post so as to view other elements of the conversation, press Enter. You ought then to be able to use the Up and Down Arrow keys to explore the other messages. To return to the timeline with which you were previously working, press the appropriate keystroke to go back. For example, if prior to pressing Enter you were viewing your Home timeline, press ALT+Windows+H. Focus should return to the appropriate timeline and also to your previous position in the timeline.

Viewing a Profile.

In the event you wish to view a profile of a user, when you hear the post details press Tab to reach the user name, then press Enter.

From this point, activate the Virtual Cursor with Insert+Z (or Caps Lock+Z if you are using the JAWS Laptop Keyboard layout). From here, you can use the Up and Down Arrow keys to review the bio, number of followers, etc. Don’t forget to deactivate the Virtual Cursor with the same keystroke once again to return to normal operation.

Playing a Video.

If the post contains an embedded video, open it up by pressing Enter, then press Tab to reach the “Play Video” Button and press the Space Bar. You can press the Space Bar again to pause and resume playback. Depending upon your settings, the video may already be playing. If this is so, and you cannot hear it, press Space Bar on the Unmute button.

Another way of achieving the same thing is as follows. Do not open up the post. Instead, press Tab repeatedly until you reach the total time of the video. This is displayed in the format of minutes colon seconds, such as, 3:11. From this point, press the Home key and the video should start playing. Press the Space Bar to pause and resume.

Switching Accounts.

If you have multiple X accounts, the chances are fairly high that you will wish to switch to a different one. To do this, press ALT+Windows+C. Then press the Tab key repeatedly to reach the account you wish to switch to. When the desired account is announced, press Enter.

Sending a Direct or Private Message.

Sending a direct message is one of the most difficult things you can do using the X’s interface. This section of the documentation explains how you might go about it.

  • To begin a new message, or reply to an existing one, press Control+D.
  • You are now in a search Edit Field. Type the name (or part of it) into the text edit area. This searches X for names which match your requirements. If you know the full name, type that so as to narrow the search criteria.
  • Press the Tab key repeatedly. You will reach two items. The first is a Check Box pertaining to the name and the second is a button, again containing the name. Press the Space Bar on the button.
