  • Focus returns to the search Edit Field. If necessary, you could add someone else to the conversation using the above procedure.
  • When you are ready to move to the next stage, press Shift+Tab to reach the “Next” Button, then press the Space Bar.
  • You are almost ready to compose your message, but focus is not in the correct location. To move to the “Start a New Message” Edit Field, press Control+Windows+S.
  • Now type your text and press Enter to send.
Searching.

To search for an X account to follow, press Forward Slash. Type what you would like to search for and press Enter.

A list of results is displayed. Press Down Arrow to move through the results. When you wish to follow an account, press Enter to open it.

Now, you can either press the Tab key once to reach the Button to follow the account and press the Space Bar, or to carry out other actions, activate the Context Menu by pressing ALT+Windows+F10.

Working With the Context Menu.

If a post is focused, you can activate the Context Menu on it by pressing ALT+Windows+F10. This allows you to follow or unfollow the user, mute the user so you will not see posts again, and other actions. Locate the item you would like with the Up and Down Arrow keys, and press Enter. There is in addition an item listed which is “Not Interested”. This again influences the X algorithm described above.

Taking Advantage of Nicknames.

Many people do have usernames on X which do not reflect their individual names. They can also contain emoji characters or the term, “Verified Account”. This means that it can take time for the screen-reader to announce. You can condense this spoken output through the assigning of a nickname; a short-form.

Focus on a post containing the username and press ALT+Windows+X. Check to ensure that the correct username is in the edit field and press Enter.

Next, type the abbreviated form and press Enter.

That’s it. From this point, JAWS should announce (and display in Braille) the abbreviated form. To delete any of your nicknames, press ALT+Control+Windows+X to bring into view a list of these. Find the one you want with Down Arrow and press Enter.

If you wish to share your nicknames across computers, in your JAWS Settings/ENU folder, find the file TwitterNames.ini and just copy it to the other machine.

Checking for Updates and Getting Help.

You can press Insert+H to get a list of keystrokes for X. You will notice at the bottom of the Hotkey Help screen is a link entitled “Check for Updates.” Press Enter on this link to check to see if there are any new X Script updates available. Back to Help Index.

The other JAWS scripts

1Password Scripts

This page contains free scripts for the 1Password Windows desktop client. They are offered for convenience and are not essential to the use of this app.

When the virtual cursor is active, Control+F will execute JAWS Find as many people are used to that. When not in the virtual cursor, Control+F equals Find in Vault. An alternative keystroke for Find in Vault, ALT+Windows+F, is available regardless of the state of the virtual cursor.

When searching a vault, JAWS will now echo the first result found, regardless of how many characters have been typed as part of the search.

If characters are inadvertently highlighted in 1Password as part of a secure note, JAWS will not say, Mark and End Mark.

Added spoken guidance when saving and creating a secure note together with when an item from the search results has been selected by pressing Enter.

ALT+Windows+Space will always take you back to the item list, useful when browsing secure note fields in the main 1Password app.

Control+Windows+F moves to filter by item type, such as Secure Notes or Logins.

ALT+Windows+M moves to the system’s main menu.

A Check for Updates feature is also available from JAWS Hotkey Help.

These scripts are offered without any form of technical support. It should be possible to use them with JAWS versions 2023 onward. To repeat, the installation of them is entirely voluntary.

Download the 1Password Scripts.

The following notes describe how to locate your JAWS Settings/ENU folder where all your JAWS scripts live. This will allow you to place the JAWS scripts into the required location in order that the screen-reader can use them.

  • First of all, locate the zipped archive with which you have been provided.
  • If you are using the standard unzip utility for Windows, pressing Enter will open up this file.
  • Press Control+A so as to select the contents of the entire zipped archive.
  • Press Control+C to copy the contents of the zipped archive to the Windows clipboard.
  • Press Insert+J to move to the JAWS window.
  • Press ALT+U for the Utilities menu.
  • Locate the item, Explore Utilities Folder, found on the Utilities menu and press Enter. Alternatively, press the shortcut key, letter X.
  • From the list of folders which appears, select, Explore My Settings and press Enter.
  • This is the folder you need to place the scripts into. Press Control+V to paste the content of the zipped archive into this folder. If Windows prompts you as to whether files should be replaced, press the Space Bar on the Replace All Button.
  • Finally, press ALT+F4 to close the Settings/ENU screen .

Chrome Plated Revisited: Using Google Chrome with JAWS for Windows

Fast, flexible and ready for the modern web.

Google Chrome is one of the most widely used web browsers in the world. It is used for shopping, banking, email, education, social media, streaming, research, work portals, online meetings, cloud services, document editing and almost every other kind of web-based task. Many services are designed and tested with Chrome in mind, and some web sites work best when opened in Chrome or another Chromium-based browser.

For JAWS for Windows users, Chrome is not simply another program on the computer. It is one of the main gateways to the modern web, and that is why confidence matters. If you know how to use Chrome well, you can move through web pages more quickly, manage downloads more easily, keep important sites close at hand, handle forms more effectively, understand browser settings, work with tabs, manage privacy and site permissions, use extensions, understand newer AI features, and make better decisions about how JAWS should behave on different web sites.

If you do not know how Chrome works, the web can feel more difficult than it needs to be. Chrome Plated has been designed to solve that problem. This new 2026 edition is a complete text-based training book showing JAWS for Windows users how to work with Google Chrome in a practical, efficient and confident way. It is based on the original Chrome Plated audio course from 2017, but it is not simply a transcript of that course. Chrome has changed. JAWS has changed. Web sites have changed. The way people use the internet has changed. This new edition brings the training fully up to date for 2026.

Why a New Chrome Course?

When Chrome Plated was first taught in 2017, many people were still moving away from Internet Explorer. The question then was often, “Can I really use Chrome with JAWS?” Today the question is different. Chrome is no longer the future browser people might eventually need to learn. For many people, it is the browser they already use every day.

But daily use is not the same as confident use. Many people know how to open Chrome, type an address, perform a search and activate links. That is a start, but it is not the whole story. Chrome contains many features which can save time, reduce frustration and improve safety if they are understood properly. JAWS also contains many features which make Chrome more efficient, but those features are not always obvious.

There are Quick Navigation keys, lists of links and headings, table navigation commands, forms options, Smart Navigation, PlaceMarkers, Personalised Web Settings, Quick Settings, speech and verbosity choices, commands for selecting text, Page Explorer, and many other tools which can make a difficult page more manageable. The purpose of Chrome Plated is to bring these two worlds together. It is not only a book about Chrome. It is a book about using Chrome with JAWS. That distinction matters.

A sighted person can often glance at a page and make decisions based on layout. A screen reader user needs reliable strategies. How do you find the main content? How do you work out whether a page is structured well? How do you move through headings, links, forms, tables and regions? How do you know when Chrome itself has focus and when the web page has focus? What is the best way to download a file? Where did that file go? Why did a keyboard shortcut behave differently on one site than another? Those are practical questions, and this book is designed to answer them.

Who Is the Course For?

This course is ideal for JAWS for Windows users who want to use Google Chrome with more confidence; people who already use Chrome but feel they are only using the basics; users who previously learned Chrome through older training and want a fully updated 2026 guide; anyone who has moved from another browser and wants to understand how Chrome thinks; people who want to improve their web browsing efficiency with JAWS; users who want a clear explanation of Chrome settings, tabs, downloads, bookmarks, history, forms, extensions and privacy options; trainers, support workers and technology instructors who need a structured guide for teaching Chrome to screen reader users; and anyone who wants to understand not only which keys to press, but why a particular technique is useful.

You do not need to be an advanced user. You should have a basic understanding of using JAWS and browsing web pages, but the course explains the Chrome-specific concepts carefully and in plain language.

How the Training is Delivered.

When you purchase the course, you will receive access to a secure area of our web site where the training is provided as a downloadable text book in Microsoft Word and HTML formats with no audio. This is the same approach used for our newer training books. It means you can read the material at your own pace, search the text, return to a topic whenever you need it, copy a keystroke or instruction into your own notes, and receive updated material more easily if Chrome or JAWS changes.

The course is written in practical, step-by-step language. It does not assume that the user can see the screen. It describes how to reach features, what JAWS is likely to report, what the controls are for, and which techniques are most efficient.

What Makes Chrome Plated Different?

There are many web browsing tutorials on the internet. Very few are written specifically for JAWS users, and fewer still explain how Chrome and JAWS work together in daily situations. Chrome Plated is not a list of Chrome features copied from a help page. It is a practical guide to using Chrome when speech and keyboard access are your primary ways of working.

The book includes practical explanations of tabs, windows, downloads, bookmarks, history, search engines, forms, tables, Chrome settings, JAWS settings, extensions, passwords, Autofill and AI-assisted browsing. It does not simply tell you that these features exist. It explains how to reach them from the keyboard, why they matter, when to use them, and what to try when a page or control does not behave as expected.

The aim of the course is practical web browsing, efficient JAWS use, clear explanations, less guesswork and more confidence.

AI, ChatGPT and the Modern Web.

Artificial intelligence is becoming part of the browsing experience. Chrome Plated therefore includes discussion of AI features in and around Chrome, including Gemini in Chrome, AI Mode, Help Me Write, AI-assisted tab organisation, Page Explorer in JAWS, and browser assistance through ChatGPT. Availability can depend on country, account type, subscription, language, Chrome version and organisational settings, so the course is careful to explain what may vary.

For blind users, these tools are worth understanding. AI may help summarise difficult pages, explain unfamiliar information, compare material from more than one source, identify possible controls, or help you decide where to go next. At the same time, AI can be wrong, and browser content may be private or sensitive. Chrome Plated explains why these tools may be useful, where they fit into a modern browsing strategy, and why the user must remain in control.

The course runs to approximately 450 pages.

Why This Course Matters.

The web is not optional. Almost everything now has a web component. Banking, shopping, healthcare, government services, email, travel, entertainment, learning, work and communication all depend on web access. For JAWS users, learning a browser well is therefore one of the most valuable technology skills you can build.

Chrome Plated is designed to help you move beyond basic browsing. It shows you how to use Chrome efficiently, how to make sense of its settings, how to manage common tasks, and how to use JAWS features which make web pages easier to understand. It also introduces newer AI features around Chrome, including AI Mode, Gemini, Page Explorer and ChatGPT browser assistance, so users understand where these tools can help and where judgement is still needed.

The course also encourages good judgement. Sometimes Chrome is the right browser. Sometimes another browser may be worth trying. Sometimes a web page is badly designed. Sometimes a JAWS setting can make the page easier. Sometimes the best solution is not a new command, but a better strategy. This course aims to teach those strategies. It is not only about pressing keys. It is about knowing what to do when the web behaves as expected, and what to try when it does not.

Price and Availability.

The cost of the training course is 60 pounds or $80 US.

You can also send an Email to brian@hartgenconsultancy.com and an invoice can be sent to you.

Conclusion.

Chrome Plated is for JAWS for Windows users who want to browse the web with more confidence, speed and understanding. Whether you are new to Chrome, returning to it after some time, or using it every day without feeling fully in control, this course gives you a structured route through the browser and the JAWS tools which support it.

The original Chrome Plated helped people make the move into a new browsing world. The 2026 edition is designed for the web we use now. Chrome Plated is back, fully revised, text-based, and ready for 2026.

Customised Scripting with JAWS

Making Technology Work the Way You Do

Are you a JAWS user struggling with an inaccessible application?

Do you find yourself wasting time on repetitive steps or searching endlessly for key information on the screen?

Would you like to move through a website or browser-based program quickly and have important sections spoken automatically?

Or are you an employer who needs to ensure a visually impaired colleague can work efficiently and independently?

If so — you’ve come to the right place. These are exactly the kinds of challenges Hartgen Consultancy solves every day.

Why JAWS Scripting?

JAWS scripting can transform how blind and visually impaired people interact with technology. It goes far beyond simply reading what’s on screen — it creates intelligent, customised communication between JAWS and almost any application.

Whether it’s a desktop program, a browser-based system, or a complex internal database, JAWS scripts can:

  • Simplify complex tasks.
  • Automate repetitive actions.
  • Provide clear speech and Braille feedback.
  • Add shortcut keys for faster navigation.
  • Enable true independence and productivity at work or home. Hartgen Consultancy is recognised worldwide for reliable, user-centred scripting. Our solutions are used by individuals, government departments, major corporations, and international organisations. We also provide scripting services to other accessibility specialists who rely on our expertise.

The Hartgen Consultancy Difference

Our scripting isn’t just about making things work — it’s about making them work well. We develop scripts tailored precisely to your needs, ensuring a natural, efficient, and enjoyable experience with your chosen software.

We have created solutions for a wide range of environments, including:

  • Microsoft Teams and Zoom.
  • Slack and Google Workspace apps.
  • Bespoke Microsoft Access and SQL databases.
  • Call centre systems and soft-phone environments.
  • Browser-hosted enterprise applications and portals. When applications change, so must their scripts. Many clients choose a support retainer to ensure that if updates break functionality, fixes can be made quickly. We can also provide guidance to IT departments on how to back up JAWS scripts for disaster recovery or machine rebuilds.

What Is a JAWS Scripting Assessment?

A JAWS Scripting Assessment is the first step toward full accessibility. It allows us to test your application, identify accessibility barriers, and determine the best scripting approach.

During the assessment:

  • We install JAWS on a suitable computer and examine how it interacts with your software.

  • We work with a knowledgeable staff member who can demonstrate the tasks the JAWS user needs to perform.

  • We gather input from the JAWS user to understand their current skill level and specific needs. Following this, we provide a detailed written report explaining:

  • Where JAWS performs well.

  • What accessibility issues exist.

  • The recommended actions to make the program fully usable. This report gives you a clear path toward a working solution — whether you’re an individual user, an employer, or an accessibility consultant.

Assessment Pricing

There are two assessment options:

  • Individual and Student Rate: £240
  • Commercial Rate: £595 Once the assessment has been completed, we will discuss the scope of scripting work required and provide a quotation based on your specific needs.

Why Choose Hartgen Consultancy?

  • Over 25 years of professional JAWS scripting expertise.
  • Trusted by individuals, businesses, government departments, and accessibility agencies.
  • Real-world experience with dozens of modern and legacy environments.
  • Thorough, user-centred testing and documentation.
  • Competitive rates and ongoing maintenance options.
  • Speech and Braille output fully supported.
  • Guidance for IT staff on deployment and backup procedures.
  • Reliable, responsive aftercare and update service.

Ready to Begin?

Efficient Messaging Using WhatsApp and JAWS

This page contains a text transcript of the majority of the presentation given to the American Council of the Blind’s Convention on Saturday 28 June 2025, entitled Efficient Messaging Using WhatsApp and JAWS.

You can download the audio from this presentation here.

Brian Hartgen: Thank you very much and a very good Saturday morning to everybody. It’s wonderful to be presenting to you once again as part of the ACB Convention and BITS specifically. I very much hope that you’re going to enjoy what I’m going to present for you today. I’m Brian Hartgen and, for the next 50 minutes, I’m going to be talking to you about an application that I resisted using for years. I don’t know why that was, but I thought perhaps it was just another app that I needed to learn how to use and which I could well do without. How wrong can you be? But one of our product beta testers insisted that it was being widely used in his country and that I really ought to try it. That application is called WhatsApp. WhatsApp is one of the world’s most popular free multi-platform messaging applications. It allows you to send text messages, make voice and video calls, share files and images, post status updates, and more all using either Wi-Fi or mobile data.

This means that you can stay connected even if you don’t have a mobile calling plan or want to avoid expensive call charges. What makes WhatsApp especially appealing is its cross-platform compatibility. It works seamlessly on both smartphones and computers, including Windows, Mac, iOS, and Android. That means that you can start a conversation on your phone, then continue it later on your desktop or laptop, for example. A feature that’s particularly useful for those of us who you screen readers and to prefer a full keyboard for typing. Another benefit is that WhatsApp doesn’t require a username or login, it simply uses your phone number. The app can automatically detect which of your contacts are already using WhatsApp, so you rarely have to manually add people. Even if your phone is turned off or offline temporarily, WhatsApp stores messages securely on its servers and delivers them the next time you open the app.

This ensures that you won’t miss important messages and you won’t be constantly checking your device out of fear of missing something. As of 2025, WhatsApp has over 2.7 billion active users globally. I can’t even imagine what that’s like, making it the most widely-used messaging app in the world. It dominates markets particularly in Europe, South America, Asia, the Middle East, and Africa, often replacing traditional SMS or phone calling entirely. You might remember the days of MSN Instant Messenger, does that bring back a memory for you? How good that was in terms of being able to send and receive instant messages? Also, how accessible it was. My wife and I got to know each other by using MSN. That was the way that we were communicating with each other. WhatsApp is very much like that, it is one of the best communication apps that we have available today.

Those of you who have attended any of my training courses or who have heard my previous presentations will know that I don’t just like using apps in their native form. I like to be very efficient at using them, I like to create scripts for JAWS for Windows, so that I can get around them faster. That is the case with WhatsApp. This particularly helps when I present, for example, my shows for our internet radio station. We have a WhatsApp group pertaining to the station and I need to keep very much on top of the messages which come in, so that I can handle them very quickly and read out the messages on air. The app needs to be littered with shortcut keys and efficient ways of working, so I created the JAWS WhatsApp scripts. You will now find some basic WhatsApp scripts within JAWS by default, but I did create them first, and if I can say so, the scripts from our company provide a far greater range of features and shortcut keys than those in JAWS out of the box.

What I want to do here is to give you an introduction to WhatsApp and how efficiently it can be navigated, and maybe by the end of the presentation, you’ll give it a try if you haven’t used it already. In order to use WhatsApp on your Windows computer, there are a few things that you need. First of all, a cell phone containing the app for WhatsApp, which you can download from the appropriate store providing apps for your individual phone. Optionally, the JAWS scripts for your computer, which I will talk about later, and finally, the app for Windows itself. There are two apps you could potentially download and instal from the Microsoft store, WhatsApp and WhatsApp Beta. As you might imagine, WhatsApp Beta contains the latest innovations, so if you want to live on the cutting edge, you can use that. I would demonstrate how to download and instal WhatsApp from the Microsoft store, but I don’t think I’ve got time to do that and I want to get to the good stuff.

I’m going to assume that you’ve been to the Microsoft store, you’ve pressed Control F in order to find an app, you type “WhatsApp” or “WhatsApp Beta,” and then you press enter and you should be able to find it right there. It’s a very simple process. To tab to the app itself, press enter on it and then you’re going to tab to the “Instal” button. This is, of course, assuming that you are signed into a Microsoft account. You’ll then get a Windows notification within a minute or so to detail the fact that the app has been installed. When you start WhatsApp or WhatsApp Beta for the very first time, there is a procedure where you need to link WhatsApp from your phone to the computer. However, fortunately, this is a totally accessible process. It didn’t used to be, but it is now.

It involves using your phone number as the linking mechanism, and I’m going to describe how you do it. Here are the steps involved to be used on your phone. Select the “Settings” tab at the bottom of the screen, select “Link devices,” select “Link a device.” Authenticate that you want to do this either by typing your PIN through touch ID or face ID. I’m going to leave the phone there at this point, because we’re going to go to the computer now. I’m going to go to the start menu.

I do realise that the speech output from the iPhone was very fast there, but including it is almost inconsequential, because it was just to verify that the code had been entered successfully. How do you communicate with people using WhatsApp? The best way is to add them to your regular contacts on your phone. When you add a person’s phone number to your contacts in the normal way, and if they are on WhatsApp, you will immediately see their names when you want to start a conversation with them. I will show you how to do that later on. Alternatively, you can join a WhatsApp group or community. A group is typically a group of people who share a common interest. That can be, for example, a group of family members who want to talk to each other, perhaps to plan a holiday or something similar, or as I say, it can be a group of people who share a hobby or interest they would like to discuss.

You can have up to 1,024 people in a WhatsApp group. A community is a collection of groups under one umbrella. Up to 50 groups can be part of one community, with 5,000 members in total. Our company provides the scripts for WhatsApp and there are two versions of them. You can purchase them to instal into most modern JAWS versions as a standalone product. However, if you have our Leasey product, which contains a vast range of tools, utilities, and services to help JAWS users, the WhatsApp scripts are included already. The WhatsApp screen contains a number of controls through which you can press Tab and Shift Tab. The primary components are a series of buttons such as “Create new conversation,” “Conversation info,” “Video call,” and so on. There are two list boxes which you’re going to interact with. The first of these shows the conversation threads available. JAWS refers to this as the “Chats list.”

The second is a list of messages in that conversation that you have selected. The scripts refer to this as the “Messages list.” There’s also an edit field for typing a message to the person in the focus conversation. Because there are quite a number of such controls to move through, keyboard shortcuts have been provided as part of the scripts to directly move to key areas of the application. Some of these are as follows. To move to the typing edit field from within a conversation is Alt T. To move to the chats list, it’s Alt C. To move to the messages list, it’s Alt M, to record a voice message, which I’ll get to later, that’s Function Key F1. This does not have a mnemonic keystroke, such as Alt R, and the reason for that will become apparent later. Audio or voice call is Alt A, video call is Alt with V. You can obtain a complete list of all of the keyboard shortcuts by checking the scripts help section, which is Insert with H. Let’s just demonstrate some of that.

Brian Hartgen: Just to recap for a moment, when you are inside a conversation, you can press Alt M to access the list of messages in that conversation directly. You can then use the up and down arrow keys to move through the list to review the activity. You can press Function key F9 on any of them if you want to review that message word by word or character by character. Now, when you press Alt M, the focus will not be at the top or the bottom of the list. The scripts contain special coding, so that you are placed at the point in the list that you last accessed. The default JAWS scripts do not do this. This is actually very useful, because if you have been examining messages in a conversation within that list and then you decide that you want to do some typing, you can then press Alt T to move to the typing edit field. Type what you want to say and press Enter, and I realise we haven’t covered some of this yet, and then you can press Alt M and you’ll immediately be back to where you were.

You can also press Control with 1 through to Control with 9. That will move between the different conversations that you’ve got open. In other words, the first nine conversations as they appear in order within the chat list. I think the first one on my chat list is Brian Dalton, so I could always press Control 1 in order to get to that conversation. Rather than tabbed pages, this is a list of settings categories. When you reach the list box, arrow down to the category you want and press Enter to move to the settings group. Notable options include, in the General category, the ability to change your name or status. The status button is labelled “About” and usually contains a one-line summary of something you wish to add to your name, such as your current mood. Other important options in settings include the kind of notifications you would like when specific events occur, setting your speakers and microphone for calling—which can be found in the Video and Voice category—and a list of keyboard shortcuts, many of which you already know. I have covered about 60% of what this application is capable of doing, and I’m afraid I’m almost out of time, but it is worth saying that, if you’d like to use ChatGPT within WhatsApp, OpenAI now provides an official way to do this through a service called 1800-ChatGPT. To get started, simply add the phone number 1800-242-8478 to your WhatsApp contacts.

That is 1800-242-8478. Once you’ve saved the number, open WhatsApp and send it a message. No account is required to begin chatting. Using ChatGPT in WhatsApp has several advantages, especially for those who prefer a simple and familiar interface. You can ask it questions, get help with writing, explore ideas, or have general conversations, or within the same app you already use for messaging friends or family. It’s also a great option for blind users, because it doesn’t require installing anything new or navigating unfamiliar websites. Everything happens in a standard WhatsApp chat, which works well with JAWS. It’s important to note, however, that ChatGPT on WhatsApp cannot give you real-time or live information, such as current news headlines or sports scores. Unlike some versions of ChatGPT that can access the internet or perform live searches, such as that found in our Leasey product, the WhatsApp version currently relies on its built-in knowledge, which may be a few months out of date.

While it’s excellent for general questions and practical tasks, it won’t be able to tell you today’s weather or breaking news. Now, I did say that you could use ChatGPT without an account, and you can, but you can also link your own ChatGPT account to WhatsApp if you have one. What are the advantages of doing that? The responses will be slightly faster, not too much faster, but a little. If you have set up custom instructions in your ChatGPT account on the web, these will be preserved when communicating with the service through WhatsApp. If you’ve taught it the way that you like to do things or the ways in which you would like information presented, you would get access to those facilities in WhatsApp. Similarly, as you will know if you’ve taken part in any of my AI training courses, ChatGPT can remember things if you have conversations with it.

Those memories too are available to you through WhatsApp. The process for linking WhatsApp to ChatGPT is not particularly well-documented, but I will go through it with you quickly. First, make sure that you have opened up ChatGPT in your web browser and that you are signed into your account. Next, browse to this link, chatgpt.com/link/whatsapp. You’ll be asked if you would like to use WhatsApp to open the programme, select “Yes.” You’ll then receive a message in your WhatsApp account, which will contain a link. Activate the link by tabbing to it and pressing Enter. Finally, consent to the fact that you would like WhatsApp to communicate with ChatGPT. That is all you need to do.

End of Presentation. Questions then followed.

The Future of the WhatsApp Scripts for JAWS

Hi to all

You will know from past discussions that a new web-based version of the WhatsApp application was in production.

WhatsApp is an application on which many of us have come to rely upon for keeping in touch, participating in groups and for work purposes in some cases.

While it was accessible, I created JAWS scripts for this application which are available as part of our Leasey product and for sale separately.

I began work on this project in May of 2022. It has taken therefore over three years to perfect the highly efficient messeging application many of us use daily.

The new web-based version has started to roll out to some people. We have one machine currently where this can be tested on a limited basis. If you find that your existing JAWS access is not functioning, this is likely to be the reason. You will probably know this is going to happen because you will be requested to link WhatsApp to your computer again via your phone.

I have now begun work on the new scripts. Because this is a web-based application, ordinarily navigated with the JAWS Virtual Cursor, the process of writing scripts has to begin again. I cannot use anything which is in place now. As and when there is functionality to test, it will be tested by our beta testers first and then it will be released when everything is stable.

But for the next few months, access to WhatsApp may be a little bumpy to say the least.

The work only was started this week, but we do have:

Keystrokes to move to specific parts of the application, such as the chat list within a conversation.

Keystrokes to make audio and video calls, to output the name and status of a contact, etc.

The sound which plays out when a message is sent.

Message reading keystrokes, such as ALT+1 to read the most recent message in a conversation, ALT+2 for the next most recent, and so on.

In summary, this is new territory and the initial release of the scripts almost certainly will not contain all the functionality you enjoy currently. But over the coming months it is hoped that most of it will be restored. Updates will be announced as and when further progress is made.

Introducing PresentAble: A New Way for Blind People to Create, Check and Understand PowerPoint Presentations

There are some areas of computing where blind people have made enormous progress. We can write documents, manage email, browse the web, edit audio, communicate across social media, use artificial intelligence, manage complex information and work with many professional applications more independently than ever before.

But presentations have always been different.

A presentation is not simply a document broken into short pieces. It is a visual object. A slide has space. It has balance. It has pictures, tables, colours, fonts, reading order, speaker notes, and sometimes sound or video. A good presentation is not only about the words it contains, but about how those words, images and other elements are arranged so that an audience can follow the message.

For a blind person, that presents a very real problem. You may know exactly what you want to say. You may be an excellent speaker. You may understand your subject completely. But when you are working in PowerPoint, it can still be difficult to answer questions which sighted people can often answer in seconds.

  • Is the picture on the left or the right?
  • Does the text fit on the slide?
  • Is one object covering another?
  • Are the colours sufficiently distinct?
  • Will a screen reader read the items in the order I intend?
  • Does the slide look crowded?
  • Have I supplied descriptions for the pictures and tables?
  • Can I work with a presentation sent to me by a sighted colleague and properly understand what is there? For many years, blind people have found ways of doing the job. We have asked colleagues to check slides. We have used templates. We have kept presentations deliberately simple. We have learned a few PowerPoint techniques and hoped for the best. Some people have become extremely skilled at this. But even then, the process has often involved more uncertainty, more assistance and more stress than it should.

PresentAble has been created to change that.

PresentAble is a new product from Hartgen Consultancy, produced in collaboration with Jonathan Simeone. It is designed for JAWS for Windows users who need to create, edit, review and understand PowerPoint presentations in a way which is structured, keyboard-driven and accessible.

This is one of those occasions where the phrase “game-changer” is not being used lightly. PresentAble does not merely provide a few keyboard shortcuts for PowerPoint. It gives blind people a different way into the presentation process. It allows you to build slides using familiar Windows controls, to choose from structured layouts, to add and organise content, to include pictures, tables, audio and video, to check accessibility, to review formatting, and to export the result as a PowerPoint file.

Just as importantly, it helps you understand presentations. That matters enormously. Blind people do not only need to create slides from scratch. They also receive presentations from colleagues, employers, teachers, students, clients and organisations. Those presentations may have been designed visually, with little thought given to how they will be read by a screen reader. PresentAble gives you a more practical way of exploring that content, making sense of it, improving it and, where necessary, preparing it for your own use.

This is about independence. It is about confidence. It is about taking a form of communication which has often been difficult for blind people to control, and making it possible to work with it in a more informed and professional way.

The Personal Story Behind PresentAble.

PresentAble also has a story behind it, and it is a story worth telling.

Jonathan Simeone was born blind. He is a lawyer by trade, and much of his professional work has focused on compliance with Titles II and III of the Americans with Disabilities Act. In other words, he understands accessibility not only as a technology user, but as someone who has worked seriously in the field of disability rights and equal access.

Jonathan lives in Oregon with his wife and the youngest two of his three stepdaughters. His interests include sports, reading, writing, learning, and, more recently, what has become known as vibe coding.

He has created dozens of PowerPoint presentations and delivered them to thousands of people. He enjoys creating presentations. He enjoys delivering them. But he hates using PowerPoint.

That distinction is important.

Many blind people do not dislike presentations. They dislike the tools they are expected to use in order to create them. They dislike the uncertainty. They dislike having to wonder whether a slide looks acceptable. They dislike being dependent on someone else to check something which should be part of their own professional workflow.

Jonathan had wanted an accessible way to create PowerPoint presentations as independently as possible for more than a decade. Then, one morning, while drinking coffee and reading more about vibe coding on social media, he began exploring what might be possible. Six weeks later, he had an application which he believed could revolutionise the way he personally created, edited and viewed presentations.

He wanted to share it with other blind and low vision people who needed to create, edit and view PowerPoint presentations. He had long admired and used software produced by Brian Hartgen and sold by Hartgen Consultancy. When he realised he was building something that could allow him to create accessible presentations in an accessible way, he posted about it on Mastodon. One of the reasons he did so was that he hoped Brian might become interested in testing the app.

Brian did more than test it. He liked the app, saw its potential, and was willing to work with Jonathan to help bring it to market.

That collaboration has led to PresentAble.

Why Presentations Have Been So Difficult.

To understand why PresentAble matters, it is worth thinking about the nature of a presentation.

A Word document is usually read from top to bottom. It may have headings, paragraphs, tables and lists, but in most cases there is a clear linear order. A spreadsheet is more complex, but it is still organised into rows, columns and cells. Even a web page, although it can be complicated, usually has a structure which a screen reader can expose through headings, links, form fields and other elements.

A slide is different.

It is a visual surface. A title might be at the top. Bullet points might appear on the left. A picture might appear on the right. A table might fill most of the slide. A video might sit below a short piece of text. A decorative image might be present but not intended to be spoken. The visual order and the screen reader reading order may not be the same. Something might be placed on the slide but not obvious to the person using speech. A picture might be too small, too large or cropped in an unhelpful way. Text might run beyond the space available. Two items might overlap.

This is why the problem cannot be solved simply by saying, “Use PowerPoint with a screen reader.” Screen readers can provide access to many parts of PowerPoint, and PowerPoint itself includes accessibility features. But blind users still need a way to make decisions about layout, appearance and structure without being forced into a drag-and-drop visual process.

PresentAble approaches the problem differently.

It gives you a structured editing environment. Instead of needing to visually drag items around a slide, you work with lists, edit fields, buttons and other controls. You choose what you want the slide to contain. You choose the layout. PresentAble places the content according to that layout. You can then review, check, edit and export.

For example, if you want text on the left and an image on the right, you choose a layout which does that. If you want a title and bullet points, you choose that. If you want an image-only slide, a table slide, a video layout or a slide with more than one image or table, there are ways of doing that too. The point is that you are not expected to position objects visually by hand. You make meaningful choices through accessible controls.

Building Presentations from the Keyboard.

PresentAble has been designed around the way blind people work.

When you create a presentation, you are not dropped into a blank visual canvas and expected to find your way around. You begin with a structured environment. You can create a new presentation, continue an existing one, add slides, name slides, choose layouts, add content items and review what you have created.

A content item might be a bullet point or a paragraph. Each item can be edited, moved, removed or copied. If a slide is becoming too crowded, you can split content so that it is divided more sensibly. Speaker notes can be added so you have reminders for what you want to say when delivering the presentation.

This may sound simple, but it is powerful. It means you can think about the message first. What is this slide for? What should the audience take from it? Does it need a picture? Would a table be clearer? Should this be two slides rather than one? PresentAble gives you tools for making those decisions without requiring you to fight the visual interface at every step.

The program also includes guided speech. When you move to a control and pause briefly, PresentAble can speak a short explanation of what that control does or give you a useful command. This is especially helpful when learning the product, because you are not expected to memorise everything before you begin. Help is close to the place where you need it.

Braille has not been forgotten either. PresentAble sends guidance to Braille through JAWS. With a connected Braille display, you can review the control name, type, shortcut and hint. That is very significant for people who prefer to learn, check and work through Braille rather than speech alone.

Creating from Scratch, or Starting with Existing Material.

PresentAble does not assume that every presentation begins from a blank slide.

Sometimes you will want to start with a completely new presentation. You may be preparing a talk, a lesson, a sales demonstration, a conference session, a training course or a community presentation. In that situation, you can build the slides directly inside PresentAble.

But there are many occasions where you already have content. You may have written notes in a Word document. You may have a Markdown file containing headings and bullet points. You may have an existing PowerPoint presentation which needs to be understood, improved or reused.

PresentAble can help with these situations too.

You can create slides from typed Markdown, import a saved Markdown file, import a Word document or import an existing PowerPoint presentation. This means you can begin in the format which is most comfortable for you, then move the material into PresentAble for slide creation, editing, checking and export.

For many blind people, this will be a very natural way to work. You might draft your ideas as headings and bullet points, import them, then refine the presentation inside PresentAble. You might receive a Word document from someone else and turn it into slides. You might take an existing PowerPoint file, bring it into PresentAble, and work through it in a more accessible environment.

That last point is especially important. PresentAble is not only about authoring. It is also about comprehension. If someone sends you a presentation, you need to know what is in it. You need to know the slide titles, the text, the tables, the pictures, the notes and the structure. You may need to adjust it before delivering it yourself. PresentAble gives you a way to work with that material in a form that is far more suited to keyboard and screen reader access.

Pictures, Descriptions and Visual Understanding.

Pictures are often central to presentations. They may illustrate an idea, show a product, display a chart, convey a mood or make a slide more engaging. For blind presenters, pictures have often been a difficult area.

PresentAble lets you add images from your computer and supply alternative text. You can decide whether an image should be described or treated as decorative. You can edit an existing image entry, replace the image file, save a copy of an image, add accessible details and remove an image when it is no longer needed.

It also helps you think about how the picture fits into the slide. Cropping and image quality are not minor details. A picture may technically be present, but still not work well if it is cropped badly, positioned awkwardly or visually unsuitable for the space. PresentAble includes tools for reviewing image fit and quality. You can work with options such as fit, top, centre, bottom, left, right and custom cropping.

Optional OpenAI features can help further. If you choose to use them, PresentAble can ask OpenAI to propose alternative text for an image, suggest a crop, create an image from a written description, or review the visual appearance of a rendered slide. These features are optional and require an OpenAI API key. The main editing, checking and exporting functions do not depend on OpenAI.

This distinction matters. PresentAble is not an AI product with a presentation feature attached. It is a presentation product which can optionally use AI to help with specific tasks. You remain in control. Each paid OpenAI request is reviewed before it is sent. You decide whether to approve it. You can use PresentAble to create, edit, check spelling, add images, write your own descriptions, run local checks and export PowerPoint files without an API key.

Tables, Sound, Video and Speaker Notes.

A serious presentation often needs more than text and pictures.

PresentAble includes support for tables. You can build and edit table slides, work with headers, rows and columns, and provide descriptions. This is useful for schedules, comparisons, results, statistics, plans and other structured information.

The product also supports sound and video. You may want to include an audio example, a short recording, background sound for a particular slide, a demonstration clip or a video sequence. PresentAble provides a structured way to add media, adjust its properties, preview it, read information about it, and check how it will behave when exported.

Speaker notes are also supported. These are the notes intended for you rather than the audience. They may remind you to explain a concept, pause for questions, mention a story, describe an image verbally or introduce the next section. For many presenters, speaker notes are an essential part of delivering a confident talk. PresentAble makes them part of the accessible workflow.

Checking Before You Share.

Creating a presentation is one thing. Trusting it is another.

PresentAble includes checking features designed to help you review your work before sharing it. These checks can identify issues such as missing descriptions, potential structural problems, crowded content and other matters which may affect the quality or accessibility of the presentation.

There is a Results page where issues can be reviewed. Results have severity levels, and you can move from a result to the relevant item. This is important because a check is only useful if it leads you somewhere practical. PresentAble is not merely saying, “There may be a problem.” It is helping you locate and repair that problem.

With Microsoft PowerPoint installed, PresentAble can go further by analysing exported slides. This can report measurable issues such as text extending beyond its allotted space or objects overlapping. Those are exactly the kinds of problems which blind people may otherwise not discover until someone else tells them.

Again, this is not about pretending that software can replace every visual judgement. It is about giving blind users far more information than they have traditionally had. It is about moving from guesswork to evidence. It is about being able to say, “I have checked this presentation, I understand its structure, and I know where the likely problems are.”

Reading Order and Accessibility for Others.

A presentation may be visually attractive and still be difficult for a screen reader user to understand. One reason is reading order.

The reading order determines the sequence in which screen reader users encounter the items on a slide. If the title is read after the body text, or if a picture description appears in the wrong place, the experience can become confusing. This matters when you are sharing presentations with other blind people, students, colleagues or customers.

PresentAble allows you to review and set reading order. It also helps you supply descriptions for pictures and tables. This means the product is not only about making PowerPoint easier for you to use. It is also about helping you produce presentations which are more accessible to others.

That is a very important point. Blind people should not have to choose between independence and accessibility. PresentAble is designed to help with both.

Working with PowerPoint, Not Against It.

PresentAble exports PowerPoint files. That is essential.

PowerPoint remains the format used by countless organisations, schools, universities, businesses, charities and public bodies. If you create a presentation, there is a very good chance that someone will expect a PowerPoint file at the end of the process.

PresentAble recognises that reality. You can save your PresentAble project as your working copy, then export a PowerPoint file when you are ready to share or deliver it. The project file keeps your slides, notes, pictures and settings together so you can continue working later. The PowerPoint file is the version you give to others or use for presentation.

This separation is useful. It means you can keep editing in the environment designed for you, while still producing a file in the format other people expect.

It is also worth noting that the main editing, checking and exporting functions work without Microsoft PowerPoint installed. However, PowerPoint is required for some additional analysis functions, such as measuring exported slides, and for OpenAI review of a rendered slide. So, if you have PowerPoint, PresentAble can make use of it for deeper checking. If you do not, you can still do the core work of creating and exporting presentations.

Designed for Learning.

PresentAble is a substantial product, but it has been designed to be learned gradually.

The user guide begins with simple examples. You can create a small presentation, add an opening slide, add a slide with bullet points, edit a bullet, add a final slide, add a reminder for yourself, review the slides, save the project, run checks and export a PowerPoint file. That is exactly the right approach. You should not have to understand every advanced feature before creating something useful.

From there, you can explore more. You can create slides from Markdown, import Word documents, import PowerPoint files, manage slides, work with content items, choose layouts, add pictures, crop images, build tables, add sound and video, change formatting, set reading order, run checks, analyse exports, manage backups, compare projects and use optional OpenAI features.

There is also a Command Centre, keyboard help, guided speech and context help. These are not decorative features. They matter because they reduce the fear of getting lost. They mean you can discover commands, learn as you go and build confidence over time.

Who Is PresentAble For?

PresentAble is for blind people who need to create or work with presentations and who use JAWS for Windows.

It may be useful if you are a trainer, teacher, student, lawyer, advocate, consultant, manager, public speaker, broadcaster, technology instructor, volunteer, accessibility specialist, campaigner or anyone else who needs to communicate ideas through slides.

It may be especially useful if you have avoided creating presentations because PowerPoint felt too visual, too unpredictable or too dependent on sighted help.

It may also be useful if you already create presentations, but want more independence, better checking, better structure and a clearer understanding of what you are sharing.

And it may be valuable if you regularly receive presentations from sighted colleagues and need a better way to understand and adapt them.

Release Date, Introductory Price and Availability.

PresentAble is scheduled for release on 23 November 2026.

Hartgen Consultancy will shortly publish a dedicated product page explaining how to pre-order PresentAble.

Until the end of 2026, PresentAble will be available at the introductory price of £80 UK, approximately $107 US. This introductory offer is partly in recognition of the Thanksgiving and Christmas period. After the introductory period, the price will rise to £100 UK, approximately $133 US.

PresentAble works with JAWS for Windows. It can be installed into JAWS versions 2022 through to 2027.

There will also be a demonstration mode, allowing people to try the product before deciding whether it is right for them.

Why This Matters.

There are products which add convenience. There are products which save time. There are products which make a familiar task a little smoother.

PresentAble feels different.

For years, blind people have been told, directly or indirectly, that presentations are visual and therefore awkward. We have adapted. We have found workarounds. We have asked for help. We have created simpler slides than we might otherwise have wanted. We have sometimes delivered excellent talks while quietly worrying about what the slides looked like.

PresentAble challenges that assumption.

It says that blind people should be able to create presentations with structure, style and confidence. It says that we should be able to understand the content of slides designed by others. It says that pictures, tables, media, notes, formatting, reading order and accessibility should be part of our workflow too. It says that exporting to PowerPoint should not require surrendering control over the creative process.

That is why this product is exciting.

It has come from lived experience. It has come from someone who is blind, who has created and delivered presentations for years, who understands the frustration, and who decided that the situation could be better. It has then been developed in collaboration with Hartgen Consultancy, with the aim of making it available to the people who need it.

PresentAble is not just about making slides.

It is about making blind people more present in the presentation process.

It is about being able to create, review, refine and share your ideas with greater independence.

It is about making PowerPoint presentations feel less like something you survive, and more like something you can genuinely own.

We believe PresentAble is going to start a lot of conversations. More importantly, we believe it is going to help many blind people create and understand presentations in a way they have wanted for a very long time.

PresentAble is coming on 23 November 2026.

This should be obvious to anyone reading the above paragraphs and is in line with Hartgen Consultancy’s other products. However, to be clear, this product requires JAWS for Windows to function. When PresentAble is launched, the full documentation will be available to read online.

And for anyone who has ever thought, “I know what I want to say, but I wish I could control the slides myself,” this may be the product you have been waiting for.

What Can J-Dictate Do For Me?

JAWS Scripts for Microsoft Teams

Upgrade Scripts for Microsoft Teams Version 3!

The business world is always buzzing about which hot new collaboration platform is the best. There certainly are quite a lot of options to choose from. But one particularly useful solution stands out: Microsoft Teams. This great collaboration solution is ideal for businesses, freelancers, and just about everyone else who works in a professional team setting.

Microsoft have made great strides in ensuring the application in the most part is accessible within the context of a range of assistive technologies. For example, various statements are often sent to the screen-reader to assist with tasks. Some script files are built into the JAWS screen-reader to support Microsoft Teams. However, while the messages and procedures available are helpful, they do not improve efficiency. Our JAWS scripts for Microsoft Teams focus upon several key areas:

Providing information in a concise format so you can become ultra-efficient.

Ensuring that aspects of Teams which are not easily navigable via the keyboard are accessible.

Providing an interface which is as easy to use as possible.

And finally, there must be no compromising on speed and responsiveness. if there is any chance of a significant delay between a keystroke being pressed and receiving speech and braille output, it is probably best not to do it at all.

The scripts include these functions and more:

  • A set of Windows Notification Rules which can be imported if desired, for use with JAWS version 2023, allowing for important notifications to be condensed for both speech and Braille output. See below.
  • Control over the automatic speaking of incoming messages. As is the case with our scripts for Zoom, you can also control the kind of messages which are automatically spoken or sent to Braille. This includes information such as who has entered or left the room in a meeting, and there is an option which can be enabled to hear who has a hand raised. This is independent of the main message alert notifications; again, like Zoom.
  • Supression of unwanted “tutor-like” messages directed through Teams so you only hear items which are relevant to you.
  • Optional guided speech prompts when you move into specific areas of Teams so you know what to do when.
  • A cleaner response when navigating in and out of specific areas within Teams.
  • Keystrokes for quick actions, such as to change or review your status.
  • Much of the output which arrives from Teams has been “refined to ensure it is more intuitive. A good example would be some of the information in the Calls Tab.
  • Keystrokes to move to areas of the application which are difficult to reach with the JAWS Virtual Cursor disabled.
  • Audio cues to denote raised hand and mute status of meeting participants.
  • Dialog Boxes containing shortcut keys in Teams so you do not need to remember them, although the keystrokes are listed so you can become more efficient in the future. There is one Dialog Box per keystroke category. Select the desired action with the Arrow keys and press Enter to action it.
  • A global keystroke to start (or move to Teams) from any application.
  • Bookmark a window such as a “pop-out chat” so as to easily return to it.
  • The ability to place the details of people who have their hands raised in meetings into the JAWS Virtual Viewer for closer review.
  • A keystroke to move to the list of teams or chat messages.
  • A facility where the scripts can be updated over the internet or if policies restrict this, the installer is always available containing the most recent version, or even a zipped archive of the files if desired.
  • Highly responsive. When you press a dedicated keystroke, there is no delay before the action is carried out.
  • Full Hotkey Help available by pressing Insert+H as is Vispero good practice.
  • All speech prompts are output to Braille. It is worth spending some time discussing participation in calls and meetings.

The focus of the JAWS scripts in the meetings area is so that pressing Tab is unnecessary in order to avoid moving into unwanted territory. Keystrokes therefore exist to move to Show Participants, More Actions, Show Conversation, and more. These are also beneficial when the conventional Microsoft keystrokes to set focus to a known area fail to yield the expected results. We want to ensure that there is an oreientation point where you can return to a known area. Similarly, keystrokes exist to report the elapsed time of the meeting or call, together with the status of muted audio and video output.

If you are working with JAWS version 2023 onwards, you can take advantage of our special Notification Rules. These are designed to provide more concise information when notifications arrive. For example, in the case of Microsoft Teams, ordinarily JAWS might say: “New notification from Microsoft Teams, John Jones is calling you.” It will then go on to recite the keystrokes you can press to interact with the call. If you’re a regular user of Teams, you hopefully know how to answer the call so you do not need reminding!

With our rules in place, JAWS will say, “Teams, John Jones is calling you” and nothing further.

If a new message is received, JAWS will say “Teams, Message from John Jones” and nothing further.

Similarly in the case of Microsoft Outlook, JAWS might vocalise “New notification from Outlook, John Jones, this is a good message”, then a preview of the message.

With our rules in place, JAWS announces “Outlook, John Jones, this is a good message”.

Notification rules are in place for Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Outlook and WhatsApp.

It is imperative to state that our additional module does not in any way interfere with the default support within JAWS for Teams. This includes keystrokes already assigned. The development for both Teams and JAWS are constantly moving targets and we have a duty not to tamper with (or spoil) such functionality.

Because some aspects of Teams are tightly interwoven with Microsoft Outlook, we also include our scripts for navigating the Outlook calendar efficiently and for viewing attachments; useful for those image files you cannot easily reach. They also contain a useful function for assisting with customising the Teams Meeting Options.

Requirements.

You will need:

  • Access to Microsoft Teams. This is usually part of a Microsoft Office subscription. If you are part of an organisation deploying Teams, you are likely to have access to more features than are available to individuals.
  • JAWS version 2021 or above. JAWS 2026 is highly recommended! The cost of this package is £70 which is currently $98 US. Updates to the scripts thereafter are free for at least a period of one year.

If you are part of an organisation wishing to purchase ten units or more, there is a very substantial discount on the cost. Please contact us for details.

JAWS Scripts for WhatsApp Classic

This application is being phased out and the developers are gradually moving people to WhatsApp Web.

WhatsApp is a popular, free, multi-platform messaging app that lets users make video and voice calls, send text messages, share their status, and more with just a Wi-Fi connection. Part of what makes this app appealing is that it works on various phone and computer operating systems, so you can continue your conversation anytime, anywhere. It can also take advantage of Wi-Fi and cellular data to make one-to-one or group calls, reducing the need for expensive calling charges. You never miss messages, but even if you miss notifications while your phone is off, the app saves recent messages for when you re-open it.

WhatsApp can identify people in your contact list who currently use the app, so you typically don’t have to add them manually. You can also invite people who don’t have WhatsApp or connect with other users you know but who Are not on your contact list.

In 2022, our Leasey product began offering support for WhatsApp. We’re now pleased to extend the same functionality so as to support the app downloadable from the Microsoft Store. We’ve now got this to the point where our new interface is an absolute pleasure to use and where you can be super efficient when using WhatsApp.

Script Features In Brief.

  • Keystroke to toggle between whether identification is given as to whether a person is typing or recording a message. This has four conditions: Disabled, Play Typing Indicator Sound, Indicate Who Is Typing, and Play Sound And Indicate Who Is Typing. Having these options on a quick keystroke is ideal because there will often be situations where you will want to disable this functionality.
  • Keystroke to enable or disable the automatic speaking of incoming messages as they arrive.
  • Option to reduce the speaking of incoming messages, so as to remove the time stamp and status.
  • Keystroke to identify who is typing or recording.
  • Keystrokes to read the last 20 incoming messages. Press twice quickly to play an audio message, place into the JAWS Virtual Viewer for closer inspection or to activate the Context Menu.
  • Keystroke to identify the focused conversation and status.
  • Plenty of keystrokes to move around the WhatsApp interface quickly without having to press Tab and Shift+Tab.
  • Keystrokes for ending a call and learning if the microphone is muted or if the camera is enabled.
  • Option to set a nickname to reduce spoken output for a long name or phone number.
  • Keystrokes for working with attachments.
  • Keystroke to virtualise profile information, ideal for obtaining the user’s phone number.
  • Keystrokes for managing aspects of recording, such as Pause and Send. We ensure that speech output from JAWS does not intrude into the recording.
  • A keystroke to verify whether recording is in progress or has been paused.
  • Sounds to indicate important status, such as when a message is sent, when recording is started or paused and to denote audio messages when moving through a Chat List.
  • A dialog box when you cancel a voice message to ensure you do not accidentally discard it.
  • Hotkey Help.
  • The ability to bring into view a list of links in the chat.
  • Update Facility.
  • Supports most modern versions of JAWS, not just the latest.
  • Full documentation.
  • And More. Hear an Audio Demonstration of the Scripts in Action!

The scripts are priced £30 which is approximately $37.

JAWS Scripts for X

Since the demise of the majority of the specialist third party clients to support the X social networking tool, people have been attempting to navigate the official web site or Windows app with varying degrees of success. It is achieveable but very unsatisfactory. There is a great deal of additional verbosity, there is no way of discerning how many characters of a tweet have been typed and there is the need to move in and out of the JAWS Forms Mode frequently, to name but three aspects.

Third party X clients made it possible for screen-reader users to access the social network in a convenient and efficient way. While those days are gone, we can at least improve the experience somewhat by a set of JAWS scripts to support both access to the X web site or app. Through the use of more logical shortcut keys and a little creativity, we have a solution which at the very least will allow you to access X with some logic and efficiency.

The JAWS scripts include:

  • Easy to remember shortcut keys, such as Up and Down Arrow to move through tweets, Control+N to compose a new tweet, Control+R to reply, Control+Shift+R to retweet, Control+Shift+Q to retweet with quoting, etc.
  • Abbreviated Mode which will condense what you hear (or see in Braille) as you move through tweets. For example, the default output for a tweet when browsing the X web site, even with its dedicated shortcut keys, might be as follows: “BBC Breaking News @BBCBreaking 57 minutes ago Mobile phone giant Vodafone to cut 11,000 jobs globally over three years”, etc, whereas Abbreviated Mode would give you, “BBC Breaking News Mobile phone giant Vodafone to cut 11,000 jobs globally over three years”.
  • Easy to remember keystrokes to move to core sections of X, such as Home, Mentions, Direct Messages, to switch accounts and more.
  • A keystroke to activate the Context Menu for a tweet, so as to carry out common tasks in relation to it, such as Unfollow or Mute a user.
  • A keystroke to copy the focused tweet to the Windows Clipboard.
  • Scan images in posts quickly via Picture Smart or Be My Eyes.
  • Assign nicknames or short-forms to usernames which may be lengthy or contain emoji.
  • Open a profile and focus is set to the correct location with the Virtual Cursor activated.
  • Full list of keystrokes in the JAWS Hotkey Help.
  • Documentation to provide descriptions of how to use the various functions.
  • Online Update facility. Hear a demonstration of the scripts in action!

Important Notes.

  • Users of our Leasey product do not need to purchase these scripts as they are included already.
  • The JAWS scripts for X in no way violate X’s Terms of Service. The cost of the JAWS scripts for X is £30 which is approximately $38 US.

Learn JAWS Scripting From Scratch

Introduction.

Have you ever wanted to learn how to write scripts for the well-known screen-reader JAWS for Windows? Do you work with an application which is only partly

accessible and you would like to do more so as to improve the experience? Have you tried scripting yourself but you do not find working through help topics

or the Scripting Manual particularly easy?

If the answer to any of the above questions is yes, then why not learn scripting in our training course. The objective once the course is completed is that you will have a good understanding of scripting basics and how to go about customising JAWS to work alongside applications.

Note the term “Scripting Basics”. No prior knowledge of JAWS scripting or programming is required.

There’s nothing like having someone teaching you a topic. Now, here is your chance to learn JAWS scripting in this way.

The major criticism of JAWS scripting is that some of the concepts are difficult to understand. The primary goals for this training course are:

  • To simplify matters further so as to provide the concepts to ensure applications are accessible.
  • Reducing spoken output in specific applications so as to become more productive overall.
  • Automating common routines. Scripting isn’t just about making applications accessible. It can be about creating more convenient ways to carry out computing tasks, reducing speech output, gathering information and presenting it in a form more easily readable, and much more.

What Do I Get?

Optional Free Scripts for FastPlay

FastPlay is an excellent audio application hosting a range of features. At present it can be downloaded from:

Portable Version.

Full Installer.

While it is completely accessible as you would expect, there is a difficulty when using FastPlay with JAWS. When holding down the Left and Right Arrow keys continually, then releasing them, it can take time for the audio processing to catch up with the focused location. This is due to a difficulty with audio applications and JAWS keyboard processing.

These scripts remedy that issue. In addition, ALT+Shift+T will report the current time in hours, minutes and seconds format, as is the case with Hartgen Consultancy’s scripts for Winamp and VLC. Control+Shift+T speak the remaining time.

These scripts are offered without any form of technical support. It should be possible to use them with JAWS versions 2023 onward. To repeat, the installation of them is entirely voluntary.

Download the FastPlay Scripts.

The following notes describe how to locate your JAWS Settings/ENU folder where all your JAWS scripts live. This will allow you to place the JAWS scripts into the required location in order that the screen-reader can use them.

  • First of all, locate the zipped archive with which you have been provided.
  • If you are using the standard unzip utility for Windows, pressing Enter will open up this file.
  • Press Control+A so as to select the contents of the entire zipped archive.
  • Press Control+C to copy the contents of the zipped archive to the Windows clipboard.
  • Press Insert+J to move to the JAWS window.
  • Press ALT+U for the Utilities menu.
  • Locate the item, Explore Utilities Folder, found on the Utilities menu and press Enter. Alternatively, press the shortcut key, letter X.
  • From the list of folders which appears, select, Explore My Settings and press Enter.
  • This is the folder you need to place the scripts into. Press Control+V to paste the content of the zipped archive into this folder. If Windows prompts you as to whether files should be replaced, press the Space Bar on the Replace All Button.
  • Finally, press ALT+F4 to close the Settings/ENU screen .

Pass The Word: 1Password for Individuals with JAWS for Windows

Your passwords are only the beginning.

Every week, we hear about data breaches, hacked accounts, scam emails and people losing access to services they depend upon. The usual advice is familiar enough: use strong passwords, make every password different, and never reuse the same details on more than one web site. That is excellent advice, but it is also impossible to follow reliably if you are trying to do it all from memory.

That is where 1Password comes in.

1Password gives you a secure, encrypted place to store the information you need to protect and use every day. It can create strong passwords, remember them for you, fill them into web sites, warn you about weak or reused passwords, and help you move towards newer and safer ways of signing in, such as passkeys.

But this course is not just about passwords. In fact, one of the biggest misconceptions about 1Password is that it is only a password manager. It is much more than that. 1Password can also store secure notes, credit and debit card details, bank account information, identity details, passport information, medical records, membership numbers, reward programmes, software licences, wireless router information, documents, important files and more.

For JAWS for Windows users, however, getting the best from 1Password can take a little guidance. Some people find the desktop app difficult to navigate at first. Others are unsure how the browser extension works, when to use the keyboard shortcuts, or how to make 1Password fit naturally into the way they already work online.

Pass The Word has been designed to solve those problems.

This training course will show you how to use the 1Password desktop app and browser extension with JAWS for Windows in the easiest and most efficient way possible. The aim is not simply to describe features, but to help you feel confident, organised and in control when working with your most sensitive information.

JAWS scripts are included with the training to make navigating the 1Password desktop app easier and more efficient. Also included are pages so you can practice storing fictitious passwords and identity information. There is also a tool to simulate using a password for use within a standalone application.

A special emphasis is placed on Quick Access, one of the most powerful features of 1Password. Quick Access allows you to find, open, fill, copy or use items from almost anywhere in Windows without first having to work through the full desktop app. Used well, it can become the fastest route to the information you need.

Who Is the Course For?

This course is ideal for:

  • JAWS for Windows users who are new to 1Password and want a clear, accessible starting point.
  • People who already use 1Password but feel they are not getting the most from it.
  • Anyone who finds the 1Password desktop app or browser extension difficult to navigate.
  • Users who want to improve their online security without making everyday tasks slow or complicated.
  • People who want one secure place for passwords, notes, cards, documents, personal records and other important information.

How the Training is Delivered.

When you purchase the course, you will receive access to a secure area of our web site where the training is provided as a downloadable text book in Microsoft Word and HTML formats with no audio.

This approach allows the material to be updated quickly as 1Password changes. It also means that new sections can be added easily if particular features, settings or workflows need attention in future.

The course is practical, structured and written in clear step-by-step language. It focuses especially on the Windows desktop app, the browser extension and the JAWS techniques which make the experience smoother.

Why This Course Matters.

1Password can save time every day, but the real benefit is peace of mind.
